Part 01 · Overview

The levers PetWise controls take EBITDA to about $6.2M, short of its target.

PetWise loses about $6.7M this year once the one-time tariff refund is taken out. Fifteen levers it controls, weighted for risk, take 2028 EBITDA to about $6.2M, and to about $12.7M if each one lands in full and on time. Reaching $10M needs the 2027 launches to work and more of each lever delivered than today’s evidence supports.

The autumn has improved, and five findings still need watching.

Part 02 · Starting point

PetWise starts next year from a loss of about $6.7M before refunds.

Before any lever is pulled, this part sets the starting line: what the business sells, what it earns once the tariff refund is taken out, where the complexity sits, and what the autumn numbers say.

This year looks profitable because of a one-time tariff refund.

Sales peaked in 2021 and have slipped every year since. This year PetWise will report a small profit of about $0.3M, but $7.4M of it is a one-time tariff refund. Take the refund out and the business loses about $6.7M. That loss is the real starting line for everything in this plan.

Three things explain most of the gap. Online sales halved. A few hundred items do nearly all the work while a long tail loses money. And each budget assumed a rebound that did not come.

The autumn has been better. Retailers are restocking, more of their orders are being filled, and shipments since 1 October are running about 10% below forecast. That is real progress. Two things temper it. Shoppers are still buying less than a year ago, so part of what shipped is sitting in retailers’ warehouses. And the margin on those shipments is running below the forecast.

Net sales have fallen by almost half since the peak.

Net sales peaked at $243M in 2021 and are about $132M for 2026 on the latest view, with actuals to September and the last quarter at forecast. The decline steepened in 2024 and 2025 as e-commerce sales fell and accounts trimmed assortments. The 2026 figure includes a Costco dog-toy program of about $11M that may not repeat.

What holds. Store accounts held up better than online: Walmart, Topco and pet specialty still carry most of the volume, and Walmart was about 1% above last year to September.

What to watch. The 2026 forecast leaned on a second-half e-commerce recovery that had not appeared by October. In September e-commerce shipped $4.1M against $6.3M forecast, and PetWise brands’ sales at Walmart fell 6.7% in the latest four weeks, with stores down 9.0% (Exhibit 2.27).

Without Costco, sales to September fell about 16%. Costco bought $11.2M of goDog toys to September against $1.5M a year before, which flatters the total. Without it, store accounts fell about 13% and e-commerce about 24%, so the underlying decline is about twice the reported 8%.

Without the tariff refunds, PetWise loses about $6.7M this year.

With actuals to September and the last quarter at forecast, 2026 shows about $0.3M of adjusted EBITDA. That includes $7.4M of one-time tariff refunds booked in May, June and July, less the $1.0M of customer price concessions the forecast set aside, so on the forecast the underlying business loses about $6.1M. The forecast sets the last quarter of e-commerce 38% above the same quarter of 2025. Shipments since 1 October have run about 10% below that forecast, and they are earning a lower product margin than it assumed, so the loss is about $6.7M. Every month from July to December is negative before refunds.

What holds. Cost cuts made in 2025 are already in the base: salaried staff fell from 137 to 96, payroll ran 12% below last year to September and annualised savings reached about $6.4M.

What to watch. The refund does not repeat, so 2027 starts from the underlying loss, not the reported figure. September alone missed its forecast by $0.7M. The last quarter is half reported. The allowance for its sales runs from $0.2M to $0.5M (Exhibit 2.30), and the allowance for its margin from $0.3M to $0.4M (Exhibit 2.09). Part of the autumn rebound is retailers restocking after the stock-outs, so December is the month to check.

The year to September ran $0.7M below forecast despite a larger refund. Lower e-commerce volume, higher marketing and other operating costs outweighed lower payroll. The forecast carried about $6.3M of refunds and the year booked $7.4M, so before refunds the business ran about $1.8M behind.

A small core of items makes most sales while the tail loses money.

PetWise sold 5,423 items in FY25. Of these, 549 made 80% of gross sales, while 3,780 items each sold under $10K. 837 items lost money, costing $5.3M of gross margin.

What holds. The core is made of recognisable items: SmartyKat scratchers, Kitty Sift, the Easy Explorer carrier and FurHaven orthopedic beds.

What to watch. Some of the largest items earn little. The top FurHaven sofa bed and the organic catnip display each earned under 4% gross margin.

Sources: PetWise FY25 item-level actuals (May 2024–Apr 2025 file and FY25–26 margin analysis).

Budgets assumed growth that the base business did not deliver.

Each annual plan since 2023 set EBITDA well above the outcome. The 2026 plan carried $17.5M of new-business go-gets, 83% of them in the second half. About $3M of the store go-gets arrived and none of the $7M e-commerce go-gets did.

What holds. The 5+7 reforecast reset the base and removed most of the go-gets, which makes it a sounder starting point.

What to watch. A plan built from won business and run-rate actions, tracked weekly, is the remedy this packet proposes.

Sources: PetWise 2023 reforecast, 2024 budget, 2025 AOP, 2026 AOP and 5+7 plan.

Shipments rebounded this autumn, though they still trail the forecast.

In the twelve weeks to 14 November PetWise invoiced $11.9M of e-commerce sales, 40% more than in the same weeks of 2025 and about 22% less than the forecast. Over the latest four weeks the gap to forecast narrowed to 9%. The main reason is supply: Amazon and Chewy received about 82% of what they ordered over the twelve weeks, against 66% a year earlier.

What holds. The rebound is profitable. Contribution margin, which is sales less product cost, allowances, freight and marketing, was $2.3M over the twelve weeks against $1.3M a year earlier.

What to watch. Shoppers bought 24% less on Amazon and 2% less on Chewy in the first week of November than a year before, so part of the rebound is retailers refilling their shelves. About half of the 1,835 recently selling items show no stock in the shared warehouse. The number to watch is December shipments against the forecast.

The margin on what shipped is running below the forecast.

Product margin is gross sales less the cost of the product. Over the latest twelve weeks it was 57.7% of online gross sales, against 60.7% in the forecast and 59.8% a year earlier, and the gap has been 2.5 to 3.0 points in each window. On a last quarter of about $12.9M that is about $0.3M the forecast counts and the shipments are not earning, so the starting point carries it. Management has not yet said whether the cause is mix or unit cost. If duty and freight are reaching product cost, the gap carries into next year at about $0.4M a year for each point.

Retailers took in more than their shoppers bought this autumn.

Over the twelve weeks PetWise shipped $10.6M to Amazon and Chewy, 33% more than a year before. Their shoppers bought about 6% less, measured at what the retailers paid. The difference, about $2.1M, went into the retailers’ stock. A year ago it ran the other way: the two retailers sold about $1.1M more than PetWise shipped them. So most of the rebound in shipments is a swing in retailer stock, and next year’s budget should not count on it twice. On 7 November 27% of the units Amazon held had been there more than 90 days.

Most of the season’s online sales come after the middle of November.

Last year about 56% of what shoppers bought from Amazon and Chewy between late September and Christmas came in the six weeks from 17 November. A December week sold nearly twice an October week, and January then ran about 10% below October. Retailers are stocked for those weeks. If shoppers keep buying less than last year, December reorders will be light, and the $7.5M of shipments the forecast still expects after 14 November is the part at risk.

On the pace so far, this year ends about $6.7M in the red before refunds. The simulator opens on the pace of shipments to mid-November: a last quarter of about $12.9M of e-commerce sales against $14.8M in the forecast. Each $1M of sales missed takes about $170K from EBITDA, and each point of margin below the forecast about $130K. Move the sliders to see what a strong or weak December does to the starting line, and what that does to 2028.

Part 03 · Market and competition

The market is growing where PetWise is weakest, and rivals press on each brand.

This part covers demand and the rivals competing for it: where owners are spending, who PetWise is up against, how each brand compares, and the position each one can take.

The category is growing, so PetWise’s decline is lost share.

Owners are still spending. Pet spending rose 3.7% last year and supplies grew faster than that. What changed is where and how they buy. Most pet supplies are now bought online, cats now outnumber dogs in American homes, and shoppers either trade up for a product that does a job or trade down to a store brand.

Detail · Where to win

PetWise sits in the squeezed middle on its largest brand. FurHaven charges more than Bedsure for a lower rating, retailers’ own brands hold most of the store shelf, and Amazon’s shopping assistant now recommends a handful of well-reviewed listings. In beds, toys and litter PetWise sold less online while each category grew.

The good news is that each brand still has something its rivals lack, and most of the moves that use it are already in the plan.

Sources: NielsenIQ via GlobalPETS; APPA State of the Industry 2026; APPA State of the Pet Industry, February 2026; competitor read of 10 Nov 2026.

Owners keep spending, and the growth is online, in cat and in function.

The category is healthy. Supplies grew 4.4% last year, and in the year to July online sales of pet supplies grew 17.4% while store sales fell 2.5%. Cats rose 2.5% to 95 million last year and passed dogs, and Chewy’s hardgoods grew in the mid-teens in its latest quarter. PetWise is under-weight in each place the growth is.

What holds. The outside read since the summer points the same way as the plan: cat, function and a well-run online shelf.

What to watch. Three outside changes cut against the plan: a 12.5% duty on China goods since July, ocean freight at about three times last autumn’s level, and Petco adding its own brands in supplies. The number to watch is the 2027 ocean contract rate.

Beds, toys and pet housing shrank in stores and grew online last year.

NielsenIQ splits each pet category into store sales and online sales. In the year to December, beds fell about 9% in stores and grew about 14% online. Toys, housing, accessories and dog treats moved the same way. Litter and cat treats grew in both. No category grew in stores while shrinking online, and supplies as a whole are now more than 60% online.

In beds, toys and litter PetWise fell while the category grew online.

Set PetWise’s own online sales beside those category figures. Its bed sales on Amazon and Chewy fell 46% in 2026 to late August, while beds grew about 14% online. Its toys fell 18% and its litter products 17%, in categories that grew. Dog treats and chews are the exception: PetWise grew 8%, though the category grew faster. The periods differ, so read the direction and not the exact gap.

Amazon and warehouse clubs gained share of pet spending last year.

Amazon took 21.3% of US pet-care spending in 2025 to late November, 1.8 points more than a year before. Warehouse clubs gained 1.1 points. Pet stores, mass retailers and grocery each lost share. Within Amazon, independent sellers on its marketplace now sell more pet care than Amazon’s own retail arm: 11.2% of spending against 10.1%. PetWise sells to Amazon as a vendor. The marketplace database holds its sales through Amazon’s own retail arm and none through a seller account. Whether selling selected items as a marketplace seller would give PetWise control of its own shelf price is a question worth putting to management.

Cats passed dogs in number last year, and homes with just cats are growing.

There were 95.0 million cats in US homes in 2025, 2.5% more than the year before, and 91.9 million dogs, 0.9% fewer. Households with cats and no dog grew by 384,000 to 22.3 million, while dog-only households fell. Owners are also keeping more cats each: 16% of cat owners have three or more, against 11% in 2018. PetWise’s cat brands are the growth lever in the plan, and this is the demand behind it.

Outside changes since the summer mostly raise the urgency of the plan.

Fifteen outside readings, each with its source, set against what it means for PetWise. Most confirm where the plan is pointed. Three raise cost or shelf pressure and are carried in the landed-cost and key-account levers.

Pet supplies grow in dollars while units stay flat.

NIQ-tracked pet supplies grew 4.8% in dollars in 2025 while units fell 0.5%, so price did the work. In stores, dollars and units both fell, while online grew in both.

What holds. Total US pet spending reached $158B in 2025, up 3.7%, so the category is not shrinking.

What to watch. Durable dog and cat products are forecast to grow about 1% a year, so PetWise must take share to grow.

Most pet supplies are now bought online, and the gap keeps widening.

About 62% of US pet supplies spending is now online. Online grew 17.4% in the year to July 2026 while stores fell 2.5%. Amazon pet sales run about $1.4B a month, up about a third, with third-party sellers more than doubling.

What holds. Chewy hardgoods grew 14.4% in its latest quarter, so a branded supplier can still grow online.

What to watch. About 29% of PetWise’s own sales are online, so the business is positioned against the flow.

Cat is growing faster than dog on Amazon and in households.

Amazon cat products grew 48% over the last year against 16% for dog. Cat households rose 5% to 53M in 2025, and shelters report record cat adoptions while dog adoptions stay below 2016.

What holds. SmartyKat and Kitty Sift already hold shelf space at Walmart, pet specialty and Chewy.

What to watch. Outward Hound’s Catstages line has grown about 36% a year since 2019 and is the most direct branded rival.

Enrichment and smart products grow fastest within supplies.

Treat-dispensing cameras grew 32%, electronic toys 27% and food dispensers 20% in the year to July 2026. Treat-dispensing toys and lick mats also grew well ahead of the category. Shoppers spend on products that do something for the pet.

What holds. SmartyKat’s Hot Pursuit electronic toy grew 56% on Amazon in 2026 (Exhibit 4.71), a sign the brand can compete here.

What to watch. Smart feeders and litter devices are moving into PetSmart and other stores, which raises the bar for cat innovation.

Cheap rivals and AI assistants are squeezing the middle of the shelf.

Two forces press on a mid-priced brand. At the low end, retailers’ own brands and China-based sellers hold most of the commodity categories. At the top of the page, Amazon’s assistant shows a few products and favours the ones with strong ratings and complete listings.

What holds. Both forces reward the same things: a clear reason to pay more, a rating above 4.3 and a listing an assistant can read.

What to watch. Walmart opened its store to outside AI agents in October, so the same test now applies there. The measure to watch is the share of hero listings rated 4.3 or higher with full content.

Shoppers are moving to the cheap and premium ends of the shelf.

NielsenIQ’s consumer survey this summer found 31% of Americans still struggling financially, against 18% a year earlier. 67% say they would rather save money unless a product is clearly better, and 54% say a mid-priced product needs a clear reason to be chosen. Across packaged goods the mainstream price tier lost a point of share in a year while discount and premium both gained. Pet products held up better than most: they are one of two grocery lines where more people plan to spend more than plan to spend less. A mid-priced bed with a lower rating than a cheaper rival sits on the wrong side of this.

Store brands and China-direct sellers own the commodity end of the aisle.

Retailer brands hold 85% to 92% of mass-channel dog furniture, crates and litter boxes. On Amazon, China-based sellers hold 67% of cat beds and furniture and 61% of dog crates. Each major account is expanding its own brands in 2026.

What holds. Branded products still win where they are differentiated and well reviewed.

What to watch. Competing on price in commodity items would put PetWise against sellers with lower costs and no brand overhead.

Amazon’s shopping assistant shows a handful of products and favours strong ratings.

Amazon’s assistant narrows a search to about five products and rarely recommends one rated under 4.0 stars. The median pick carries about 3,000 reviews. Sponsored prompts have been billable since March 2026, so the assistant is also an ad channel.

What holds. Gen-AI tools can rebuild attributes, images and answers for a few hundred hero listings in months.

What to watch. FurHaven ran 977 dog-bed listings at about $3K of sales each, which splits reviews and weakens each listing’s chance of being shown.

Three kinds of rival press on PetWise, and scaled peers earn far more.

PetWise meets online-native sellers such as Bedsure, retailers’ own brands such as Frisco and Vibrant Life, and branded specialists such as KONG. Each wins in a different way: price and reviews, shelf control, or a single trusted product.

What holds. PetWise still leads or ranks second in several positions, among them carriers in pet specialty and cat products at Walmart.

What to watch. Scaled peers in the same categories earn double-digit margins, so the gap is execution, not the category. The rival move to watch is Bedsure’s advertising on Chewy, where it passed FurHaven in paid search share during October.

Bedsure passed FurHaven in paid search share on Chewy during October.

On the searches PetWise tracks on Chewy, FurHaven held 3.62% of paid placements on 1 October and 3.24% on the 31st. Bedsure went from 2.71% to 3.73%. FurHaven spent about $118K on Chewy’s site in the month. On Walmart.com, SmartyKat holds 19.3% of paid placements and 6.8% of unpaid ones, while Walmart’s own Vibrant Life holds 9.4% unpaid with little advertising. A brand that shoppers find mostly through paid placements pays for each visit.

Three kinds of rival compete for PetWise shoppers, and each wins differently.

The competitive set is the brands that appear beside PetWise’s hero items on the retailer pages and best-seller lists read for this packet. Online-native sellers such as Bedsure, EHEYCIGA and Potaroma win with one deep, low-priced listing. Retailer own brands set the price floor at Chewy and Walmart, and branded specialists each hold one proof of safety, origin or durability.

What holds. PetWise sells through more channels than the online-native sellers in the set, and FurHaven held the largest share of Chewy dog-bed sales in early 2025, at about 31%.

What to watch. Bedsure and Potaroma now list on Chewy and Walmart as well as Amazon. A move by either into stores would put the online price gap on the shelf beside FurHaven and SmartyKat. Brand shares outside dog beds are not available, so scale is shown by the evidence that exists for each rival.

FurHaven and goDog carry price premiums that their ratings do not support.

On Chewy, FurHaven’s large orthopedic sofa sells about 22% above Bedsure’s with a rating 0.2 stars lower, and goDog’s dragon sells about 22% above Chewy’s own plush with a rating 0.3 lower. Sherpa’s premium over Chewy’s own carrier is far larger, at about 173%, but Sherpa holds the top rating on Chewy. Most cat and chew items sit at or below rival prices with equal ratings. The exceptions are the SmartyKat scratcher, at about 37% above Walmart’s own, and Hot Pursuit, which is cheap and rated 0.7 stars below its closest rival.

What holds. Six of the ten hero items match or beat their closest rival on rating, so the quality gap is narrow and specific.

What to watch. The same FurHaven sofa model and size, in different colours, was $24.08 at Walmart and $57.21 on Chewy on the same day, a gap of about 58%. Gaps like this invite price matching and weaken the shelf price in each channel.

On Chewy, FurHaven is priced above Bedsure and rated below it. The map places the large orthopedic beds in stock on Chewy by shelf price and star rating. FurHaven’s sofa sold at $57.21 with a rating of 4.3, against $46.74 and 4.5 for Bedsure’s. Chewy’s own Frisco sofa read higher than FurHaven on both price and rating, though its price was read automatically and needs confirming by hand.

Scaled peers earn double-digit margins in the same categories.

Central Garden & Pet’s pet segment earned a 21.4% adjusted EBITDA margin in its latest quarter, and Spectrum’s pet care business about 20% before tariff refunds. Outward Hound, closer in size to PetWise, earns about 11%.

What holds. These peers win with focused categories, fewer sites and disciplined sourcing, which are the same levers in this plan.

What to watch. Peers are also cutting China sourcing and adding automation to logistics, so the bar keeps rising.

Each brand loses to its nearest rival on something a shopper can see.

The scorecard rates each brand’s hero item against its closest rival on six measures a shopper meets: price, rating, review depth, price consistency across retailers, Amazon search and the claim on the listing. The findings below take the brands in turn.

What holds. Kitty Sift, SmartyKat and Pet Factory hold up well. Their gaps are narrow and cheap to close.

What to watch. FurHaven and goDog carry price premiums their ratings do not support. The number to watch is FurHaven’s price gap to Bedsure on the same bed.

Kitty Sift holds the strongest position, and FurHaven and goDog the weakest.

Each brand is scored from one to five on six measures that shoppers and retailers can see: price, rating, review depth, Amazon search, price consistency and a provable claim. Kitty Sift scores 25 of 30, SmartyKat 22 and Pet Factory 20. FurHaven and goDog score 16 and Sherpa 17, and these are the three brands priced above their rivals.

What holds. Kitty Sift, the strongest, and Pet Factory are the two repeat-purchase brands, and both are growing on Chewy (Exhibit 4.69).

What to watch. Amazon category search is the common gap. Five of the six brands are absent from the best sellers for their main search term. SmartyKat is scored on its catnip mice. Scored on Hot Pursuit, its best-known toy, its total falls from 22 to 19.

FurHaven leads on Chewy but sits above the price band where Amazon sells.

In early 2025 FurHaven held about 31% of dog-bed sales on Chewy and about 4.8% on Amazon, where Bedsure and EHEYCIGA together held about 26%. About 73% of Amazon dog-bed sales were under $60, where FurHaven held between 1.7% and 3.3%, and about 57% of FurHaven’s own Amazon sales were above $60. Titles with a waterproof claim made up about 55% of Amazon sales, and FurHaven had almost none.

What holds. FurHaven states certified foam and a warranty, which the Bedsure and Frisco pages do not, and its calming donut out-rates Best Friends by Sheri’s, the best-known calming bed, on Chewy.

What to watch. Share data is from early 2025. In the agency’s tracked Amazon search set, FurHaven slipped from 20% in May 2026 to about 17% in September, while EHEYCIGA reached 19%.

FurHaven lost over half of its own brand shelf after branded spend was cut. From July 2026 branded search spend on Amazon fell about 64% while total spend rose about 29%, and FurHaven’s share of the shelf on its own brand searches fell from about 67% in June to about 30% in August. About 76% of Sponsored Brands sales on brand terms came from shoppers new to the brand, and the agency found that the lost shelf spread across many small sellers rather than one rival. 391 of 466 brand campaigns were paused in September. October’s placement data repeats the pattern: top-of-search spend fell 38% although it returned 3.99x, against 2.38x on product pages (Exhibit 7.35). The review shows lost shelf rather than a proven loss of sales. FurHaven’s Amazon decline against last year eased from about 48% in the second quarter to about 45% in July and August, and October’s fixes lifted Amazon search returns to 2.78x (Exhibit 7.30).

SmartyKat wins on value basics, but its best-known toy rates below rivals.

SmartyKat’s catnip mice cost $0.50 each with a 4.7 rating, half the price of Chewy’s own mice at the same rating. Hot Pursuit, its most-reviewed item, rates 3.7 to 4.0 and runs on batteries, while rechargeable look-alikes rate 4.4 to 4.6 at about twice the price and sell an estimated 8,000–10,000 units a month each on Amazon. Kitty Sift is the lowest-priced disposable litter box read, but Chewy’s sturdier own-brand box rates 4.6 against Kitty Sift’s 4.2.

What holds. SmartyKat scratchers carry several best-seller badges at Walmart, its lounge formats rate 4.7 to 4.8, and Kitty Sift is the one cardboard brand among Amazon’s best sellers for its searches.

What to watch. Three of five older SmartyKat listings read on Chewy were discontinued or replaced, which strands thousands of reviews. Online-native sellers such as Potaroma now list on Chewy and buy placements on SmartyKat’s Walmart pages.

goDog and Sherpa both sell above the rivals nearest to them.

goDog’s dragon rates 4.3 on Chewy from 6,300 ratings, ahead of Outward Hound, Tuffy and BARK at 3.9 to 4.1, but behind Chewy’s own plush at 4.6 for about 18% less. The ten best-selling dog toys on Amazon average $9.26, about half of goDog’s Chewy price. Pet Factory’s rolls cost $2.30 each on Chewy, between Walmart’s own brand at $1.86 and Good ’n’ Fun at $2.50, with verified US manufacture that most rivals do not state.

What holds. TrustyPup’s tough plush out-rates Walmart’s own at about two-thirds of the price, and Pet Factory is growing on Chewy with most of its sales on Autoship.

What to watch. Amazon’s “rawhide” search is led by rawhide-free products, and Pet Factory has no collagen-named or rawhide-free item. Its Chewy list price of $35.99 sits about 57% above the selling price.

Sherpa stands alone between twenty-dollar carriers and premium safety brands. Carriers of the same or a similar size to the Sherpa medium sell at $20–$29 with ratings of 4.4 to 4.8, and design and safety brands start at $145. Sherpa sells at $52.99 to $70.99 depending on the retailer and holds the highest rating on Chewy, where its price is also highest. On Amazon, Sherpa has about 8,500 ratings against 37,900 to 53,100 for the leaders, and it ranks ninth by units on its own brand search. Sherpa tops Chewy’s 2026 list of airline carriers with a 4.8 rating, and its boarding guarantee is a claim no rival read makes. The guarantee page, as read, showed one airline. Sherpa was not found on the pages of the crash-test certified list that were read, while the premium brands lead with certification. PetWise’s own TrustyPup carrier already sells at $25 with 1,796 ratings at Walmart.

Each brand has a clear position to take, and most moves sit inside the plan.

FurHaven should hold a smaller premium backed by a better rating, one price across retailers and a certified-foam claim with a longer warranty. Sherpa should defend its premium with proof, SmartyKat should fix its best-known toy and take silvervine to mass retail, and goDog should stay the premium tough plush while TrustyPup covers the value band. Pet Factory and Kitty Sift should protect strong positions with clearer claims and a collagen-named or sturdier tier.

What holds. Most of these moves are the practical content of levers already in the plan: the FurHaven reset, cat growth, the digital shelf and retail media. Management’s 2027 slate, shown to the board on 22 October, takes several of them: FurHaven+ with certified foam and warranty registration, rechargeable SmartyKat+ toys, the Chip Dips collagen chew and cat-first Sherpa+ carriers.

What to watch. Six options go beyond the plan and are not counted in its value, and the 2027 slate covers four of them at least in part. With the slate’s other launches they are the candidates for the launch reserve of about $5M tested in Odds and decisions (Exhibit 10.04). No launch carries a sales, margin or price target yet, so the reserve is a what-if size and not a sum of these options.

The first moves are specific to each brand. The table sets out the position each brand holds today, the position to take and the first moves, with the plan lever each one supports. The advantages they build on are ones PetWise already holds: certified foam, the boarding guarantee, US-made chews and the one cardboard box among Amazon’s best sellers.

Part 04 · E-commerce

Online sales fell by more than half, and most of the reasons sit inside PetWise.

This part tells the online story in one place: what happened, why, where it stands this month and what to do. The evidence is PetWise’s board documents, the marketplace database to late August, and the weekly and monthly reports to mid-November.

Online sales halved, and most of the fixes are in PetWise’s hands.

E-commerce was about 38% of PetWise’s sales in 2023. It is about 28% now. Sales went from $91.9M to about $43.3M while the same categories grew on Amazon and Chewy, so this is lost share, and FurHaven beds are most of it.

The story in 6 pictures · each opens its detail
What happened Online sales fell in each of the last three years.

Detail · Way forward

Six things went wrong, and they overlapped. FurHaven priced itself out of the band where beds sell. Stock ran out. Ad money returned less than it cost. Listings went dark. New items did not land. And the team kept changing. Most of the six are PetWise’s own to fix.

Since the summer, fill rates have recovered and Chewy is almost level with last year, while Amazon is still about a quarter down. The way forward is narrow by design: profit first, on the few hundred items that make most of the sales.

Sources: PetWise board documents, 2025–26; PetWise marketplace database; PetWise e-commerce war room, 13 Nov 2026; PetWise monthly business review workbook, October 2026.

Each plan since 2025 assumed a rebound that did not arrive.

E-commerce gross sales fell from $91.9M in 2023 to $67.8M in 2024, $48.1M in 2025 and about $43.3M on the latest view of 2026, a fall of 53%. The 2025 plan set $95.8M and the year delivered half of it. The July 2025 reforecast set $63.1M, and the 2026 plan set $55.9M, +16.5% on the year before.

What holds. The shortfall is narrowing: the latest view of 2026 sits $12.6M below its plan, against $47.7M in 2025, and $3.9M below the June forecast.

What to watch. That forecast still needed autumn shipments near double the spring pace (Exhibit 2.16), and September shipped $4.1M against $6.3M. If the last quarter misses by as much as the year to September did, 2026 ends near $41.8M. The forecast sets that quarter 38% above the same quarter of 2025, and on the pace of shipments to 14 November the year ends between $41.0M and $41.9M (Exhibit 2.30). A 2027 budget that starts from a rebound would repeat the pattern.

Online contribution fell far faster than online sales. In the twelve months to March 2024 e-commerce earned $23.2M of contribution margin, as management reports it, on $74.2M of net sales. In the twelve months to July 2025 it earned $2.4M on $44.3M. Management put the step down in late 2024 to a site closure ($1.9M), temporary labour ($1.3M), chargebacks ($1.0M) and about $5M of cancelled orders, and to retailers working down extra stock shipped in late 2023.

Most of the online decline happened in 2025, and the slide has slowed since.

Amazon shelf sales, which are what shoppers paid, were $18.7M from 1 January to 27 August 2026, against $27.1M a year earlier. Chewy shelf sales over 35 matching weeks were $13.7M against $18.2M. Most of the fall happened during 2025. Since January, Amazon has sold about $70K to $90K a day and Chewy about $340K to $480K a week.

What holds. Chewy has run level since January, and Amazon’s decline has slowed. The gap to last year narrowed from 34% in the first quarter to 21% in the latest 31 days on Amazon, and from 31% to 11% on Chewy.

What to watch. Much of the narrowing comes from easier comparisons. Amazon still drifted down during 2026, from $83K to $90K a day in January and February to about $70K in July and August, and FurHaven was still sliding month by month. The item-level data stop at the end of August. Retailer totals in the paid media dashboard run to late October: Amazon orders were about $2.1M in September and are pacing about $2.5M for October, still about 26% below the 2025 monthly average (Exhibit 4.78).

Six causes explain the online decline, and PetWise controls most of them.

Price came first: lower-priced rivals took FurHaven’s share of Amazon bedding from 2022, and in 2026 retailers raised its shelf prices again. Supply came second: PetWise shipped about 66% of what Amazon and Chewy tried to buy in 2026. Advertising was cut and then returned below breakeven, best-selling listings went dark, the range kept a long tail while launches added little, and the team and its plans changed repeatedly.

What holds. Most of these were decisions and execution inside PetWise, so they can be reversed. Stock is already improving: Chewy’s fill rate has been above 77% since July, and Amazon search returns recovered from 1.95x in August to 2.78x in October.

What to watch. No cause is fully closed. FurHaven’s sofa still sells about 22% above Bedsure’s on Chewy, 40 always-on Amazon items sell on fewer than half of days, ads return less than breakeven at each retailer, and the plan’s head of e-commerce is not yet hired. The sizes below overlap, so they do not add up.

Each cause has a size, a status and a lever that addresses it. The table sets the six causes side by side, in the order they bit. Price and stock are the two largest, and both have a lever in the plan with a named owner. The sizes are measured on different bases and overlap.

The loss sits in FurHaven, in beds and in items priced above $30.

The four cuts below tell one story. Each online channel sold less. FurHaven fell 49% on Amazon and 35% on Chewy in 2026 to late August, while the brands owners buy again and again held. Beds and habitats carry most of the fall, and dearer items fell far harder than cheap ones.

What holds. Chews, litter and treats, the repeat purchases, were level or growing on both retailers. That is where PetWise’s cat and chew brands are priced.

What to watch. Most FurHaven sales sit above $30, where rivals price lower. The measure to watch is FurHaven units against last year on each retailer.

Each of the four online channels sold less than last year.

Shoppers bought 31% less of PetWise’s products on Amazon and 25% less on Chewy in 2026 to late August than in the same period of 2025. The two seller accounts PetWise runs itself on Walmart.com and Target.com are small and also fell. Part of the fall was supply: PetWise shipped about 66% of what Amazon and Chewy tried to buy between January and September.

What holds. Chewy has improved. Its fill rate, the share of what a retailer tried to order that PetWise shipped, averaged 83% from July to September, against 62% in the first half, and its shelf sales outside FurHaven ran above last year in the latest nine weeks.

What to watch. Amazon stayed below 60% fill from June to August and reached 76% in September. The number to watch is Amazon’s confirmation rate, the share of its orders PetWise accepts, which was 71% for the nine months against 91% for store accounts.

PetWise shipped well short of what Amazon and Chewy tried to buy. Between January and September, Amazon and Chewy placed $29.4M of orders and PetWise shipped $26.1M. Counting the orders PetWise did not confirm, about $13.4M of their demand went unserved, which is 48% of the company’s unserved demand on 24% of its orders. Demand is estimated from the confirmation rate, so the figure is an estimate.

FurHaven lost the most dollars, and the repeat-purchase brands held.

FurHaven sold about $9.5M less across Amazon and Chewy, which is 74% of the two retailers’ decline. SmartyKat is the second-largest loss, most of it on a handful of Amazon listings that stopped selling. Pet Factory chews and Kitty Sift litter boxes, which owners buy again and again, held or grew.

What holds. The brands that held are the ones bought on repeat: Pet Factory was level on Amazon and grew 24% on Chewy, and goDog grew on Chewy.

What to watch. FurHaven is still the largest online brand, so its recovery decides the channel. The measure to watch is FurHaven units against last year on each retailer.

Beds and habitats carry most of Amazon’s decline, while chews held level.

Beds, crates and other habitats fell 43% on Amazon and make up 71% of its decline. Chews and feeding were level, litter fell 21% and toys 29%. The pattern is the same on Chewy: beds and gear fell by about a third while treats and litter grew.

What holds. The categories owners buy on repeat are stable or growing on both retailers, which matches what owners report: they protect food and routine care and trim other spending.

What to watch. Catnip and training items on Amazon fell from $766K to $8K as listings went dark. The measure to watch is the number of always-on items that stop selling.

On Chewy, treats and litter grew while beds and gear fell by a third. Chewy’s categories show the same split between repeat purchases and one-off purchases. Dog treats and chews grew fastest from a small base, and dog beds, crates and gear, the largest category, fell most.

Items priced above $30 lost far more than cheaper items on both retailers.

On Amazon, items that sell for $30 or more lost 44% of their sales against 23% for cheaper items. On Chewy the figures are 35% and 11%. Items above $30 account for about $8.1M of the $12.9M decline across the two retailers, or 63%.

What holds. The $15 to $30 band is the most resilient on Amazon, down 18%, and items under $30 on Chewy fell about a tenth. That is where the category’s volume sits, and where PetWise’s repeat-purchase brands are priced.

What to watch. Most FurHaven sales sit above $30, where rivals price lower. The measure to watch is the share of FurHaven bed sales priced between $45 and $65, the band the plan targets.

FurHaven sits above the band where beds sell, and retailers earn little on it.

Price is the first cause. Lower-priced rivals took FurHaven’s share of Amazon bedding, and through the summer retailers raised FurHaven shelf prices while what they paid PetWise stayed flat. Items priced up the most lost the most units.

What holds. The pattern is consistent across both retailers, across years and across items, which is why the plan starts FurHaven’s recovery with price.

What to watch. The picture changed in the autumn: Chewy is now cutting FurHaven prices at its own expense. A retailer that loses money on a brand asks for it back in terms or gives the shelf to someone else, so the reset has to be agreed and paid for on purpose.

By October retailers were cutting FurHaven prices at their own expense.

In early November Chewy’s average FurHaven price was 13% below a year earlier, its best-selling bed had dropped 20% in four weeks, and five of its ten best-selling FurHaven beds sold for less than Chewy paid. Across October about 26% of FurHaven’s Chewy sales were below cost, and Chewy and Amazon each kept about 12% to 13% of the shelf price before allowances, against a quarter to a half on the other brands.

In October FurHaven items sold more on Chewy where prices fell and ads doubled.

The account team’s list of October’s largest movers on Chewy shows what a lower price does. Three FurHaven items gained the most, and on each the price was 12% to 27% lower than in September, with ad spend at least doubled and a site-wide promotion on two of them. One goDog item gained on coming back into stock. The losers were an item out of stock, an item priced 24% higher and an item shoppers traded down from. Units answer to price and availability. The open point is who paid. These gains came with heavy promotion and advertising, so the margin on them has to be checked before the pattern is scaled.

FurHaven lost most of its Amazon bed share to lower-priced rivals.

FurHaven held 18.5% of Amazon pet bedding in 2022 and 7.0% in the year to 10 August 2024, while Bedsure rose from 11.9% to 16.3%. Amazon bedding grew 4% between 2022 and 2023 while FurHaven’s Amazon sales fell 42%, so shoppers stayed and bought brands priced below it. FurHaven is the large brand most dependent on e-commerce (Exhibit 2.14), so this loss set the base for what followed.

What holds. FurHaven remains a large bed brand. It held the largest share of Chewy dog-bed sales in early 2025 (Exhibit 3.44), and its bed sales at Walmart, where it sells at its lowest prices, grew in 2026 (Exhibit 7.14).

What to watch. On Chewy, FurHaven’s large orthopedic sofa sells about 22% above Bedsure’s with a lower rating (Exhibit 3.17), and most Amazon bed sales sit under $60, below most of FurHaven’s range (Exhibit 3.20). A move by Bedsure or by Chewy’s own brand into FurHaven’s remaining price tiers would change the view.

In 2026 retailers raised FurHaven shelf prices, and shoppers bought far fewer. On the same FurHaven items, the shelf price, which is what shoppers paid, rose about 7% on Chewy and 5% on Amazon between the 2025 and 2026 year-to-date periods, while what PetWise charged moved about 1%. Units on those items fell 32% on Chewy and 46% on Amazon. Pet Factory and Kitty Sift, where Chewy’s shelf prices eased, sold 30% and 90% more units.

Shelf prices rose on FurHaven while what PetWise charges stayed flat.

On the same FurHaven items, Chewy’s shelf price rose about 7% in a year and Amazon’s about 5%. What PetWise charged those retailers moved about 1%. Items carrying about four in ten FurHaven units rose more than 10% at the shelf, and they lost about 60% of their units on both channels.

What holds. On Chewy, FurHaven items whose shelf price stayed within 3% lost about 6% of their units. Where the price held, the volume largely held.

What to watch. On Amazon even flat-priced items lost 44% of their units, so price is not the whole story there. Why shelf prices rose is a question for management: the data cannot tell a higher suggested price from fewer funded promotions or a retailer pricing decision.

Retailers earn little on FurHaven, which helps explain the price moves.

Chewy’s margin on FurHaven, before any allowances PetWise pays, was under 1% in 2025 and about 4% in 2026. It sold more than a third of its FurHaven sales below what it paid. Amazon’s margin on FurHaven fell to about 15% over the summer after it cut shelf prices. On goDog, Sherpa and SmartyKat the same retailers earn 24% to 49%.

What holds. The other brands leave retailers a healthy margin at the shelf, and those brands held up better.

What to watch. Retailers respond to thin margins by raising prices, cutting stock or dropping listings. PetWise pays about 30% of gross sales in allowances on these channels, so there is room to move money from allowances into the invoice price without lowering its own net price.

Stock-outs, dark listings and thin content held back the items that matter.

Three execution causes sit beside price. Retailers placed orders PetWise could not fill, leaving about $13.4M of demand unserved on Amazon and Chewy from January to September. A handful of best-selling listings stopped selling. And listing content, ratings and returns trail what the best sellers in the category now show.

What holds. Each of these is cheap to fix and sits inside a lever already in the plan. Fill rates have improved since the summer: in the week to 14 November the orders PetWise could not fill were worth $147K, against $520K in the same week a year before.

What to watch. Stock is still thin: about half of the recently selling items show no stock in the shared warehouse, and orders coded out of stock over the past year were $11.3M, up 80%. The number to watch is the count of always-on items that stop selling.

Stock-outs and delistings cut orders that retailers had already placed.

Retailers place orders, and PetWise cuts the lines it cannot ship. About $5M of orders were cancelled around the late-2024 site closure, $2.5M were cut between August and October 2025, and $9.1M between January and September 2026. Management put the 2025 cuts down to a discontinuation process that removed live items and to forecasting, and the 2026 cuts to forecast error four months ahead of delivery.

What holds. Fill rate passed 85% in October 2026, and forecast accuracy improved 11 points between April and August. Chewy’s fill rate reached 94% in one week of August (Exhibit 8.08). That reading counts orders PetWise accepted. Counting the orders it declined as well, PetWise shipped about 66% of Amazon and Chewy demand from January to September, and both retailers were above 76% in September (Exhibit 4.08).

What to watch. PetWise filled under half of Amazon’s SmartyKat and Sherpa orders in September (Exhibit 4.80), and Amazon stock cover is 8 weeks against 14 a year ago. The periods in the chart differ in length, so each bar is read against its own months.

Advertising was cut hard in 2025 and came back at lower returns. Advertising fell from $6.0M in 2024 to $3.1M in 2025, and in October 2025 Amazon ad spend ran 65% below the year before with ad sales 35% lower. Management noted in September 2025 that 98% of unpaid Amazon searches in its categories name no brand, which limits searches for FurHaven by name. The 2026 forecast puts performance marketing back at $5.2M, and to September it ran 69% above 2025 while e-commerce sales fell 24%.

Listings that went dark took sales that should be quick to recover.

Five SmartyKat catnip and toy listings sold $1.4M on Amazon in the 2025 period and under $0.1M in 2026. They explain about 80% of SmartyKat’s Amazon decline. The catnip shaker alone sold on 203 days last year and on 28 days this year.

What holds. Demand did not go away. A silvervine catnip item more than doubled on Chewy over the same period, and Hot Pursuit grew 56% on Amazon and 26% on Chewy. A new SmartyKat catnip canister, launched in November 2025 and missing from the product master, sold $473K on Amazon in 2026, so part of the shaker’s loss has already come back under a new listing (Exhibit 4.71).

What to watch. Of 215 Amazon items that sold almost daily in 2025, 40 now sell on fewer than half of days, and their sales fell from $1.1M to $0.1M. The database holds no stock data, so it cannot tell an empty shelf from a suppressed listing. The paid media dashboard points to stock: PetWise filled 41% of Amazon’s SmartyKat orders in September (Exhibit 4.80).

Assortment, content, ratings and returns each hold back the listings that matter.

Four quality levers sit beside price and stock. The assortment has a long tail: 1,367 Amazon items make about 5% of its sales, and items launched since mid-2025 made about 5%. Listing content was incomplete when it was last audited. Ratings trail rivals on the hero bed and the hero cat toy, and FurHaven’s Amazon return rate rose from 7.4% to 9.2% of units.

What holds. These levers are cheap to pull and sit inside levers already in the plan: the digital shelf, the content factory and the item cut. They need an owner and a weekly list, not new spending.

What to watch. The content audit dates from March 2025 and covers one of the two Amazon accounts, so it needs re-running. The number to watch is the share of the 257 Amazon hero items rated 4.3 stars or higher with full content.

Most audited listings lacked video, and many lacked a full image set. An audit of 3,564 Amazon listings in March 2025 scored the average item 64 of 100 for content, and 81 when weighted by sales, so the best sellers were in better shape than the tail. About 31% of items carried a video and 54% had seven or more images. Half of FurHaven’s rated items sat under 4.3 stars, carrying about 23% of its sales.

Fill rates have recovered and Chewy is nearly level, though Amazon still trails.

This is the read to mid-November. In the first week of the month shoppers bought 24% less on Amazon than a year before and 2% less on Chewy, where units were up 13%. PetWise’s own shipments are running well ahead of that, 40% up on last year over twelve weeks, as retailers rebuild stock.

What holds. Sherpa is up 40% on Amazon, goDog is up 43% on Chewy, and FurHaven’s gap on Chewy has narrowed each month this year.

What to watch. On Amazon the problem is conversion as much as traffic. In October more shoppers viewed PetWise items than a year before and far fewer bought, and in the first week of November traffic was 21% below last year. Each click also costs more than a year ago, so the recovery cannot be bought with ads. The number to watch is FurHaven on Amazon, still 38% down.

Amazon and Chewy now receive far more of what they order than in the summer. Dollar fill, the share of ordered value that PetWise confirms and ships, was 76% on Amazon and 86% on Chewy over the latest twelve weeks, against 62% and 70% over the past year. Both are still below the 90% the plan needs, and the latest week slipped to 82.5% from 89.5%.

In October FurHaven and SmartyKat still fell on Amazon while most brands grew on Chewy.

Item by item, October sales on Amazon were about 10% below the same items a year earlier and about 5% below on Chewy. FurHaven fell on both. SmartyKat fell by a third on Amazon, where several listings are still dark, and grew on Chewy.

Shipments to Chewy turned from steep falls to growth in July.

PetWise’s invoices to Chewy ran 42% below last year from January to June, about $5.5M less. From July to November, counting orders still open, they are running 45% above, about $2.8M more. That is the fill-rate recovery showing up in orders. Two cautions sit beside it. Chewy’s shoppers are still buying slightly less than a year ago, so the growth is Chewy refilling its shelves. And the forecast ran ahead of it: in October Chewy placed $1.5M of orders against $2.7M in the forecast, so about 91% of the month’s miss came before any order was placed.

On Amazon more shoppers looked in October and far fewer bought.

Amazon’s own figures for October show views of PetWise items 11% above a year earlier and units bought per view down 31%, from 14.2% to 9.9%. Prices averaged 9% higher and sales fell 16%. PetWise held the buy box on 98% of views, so the items were there to buy. Shoppers looked and chose something else. That points at price, rating and content, which is the work of the digital-shelf lever, and not at traffic.

The decline has eased since the first quarter, least at FurHaven.

Against the same weeks of 2025, Chewy shelf sales were 31% lower in the first quarter of 2026 and 11% lower in the nine weeks to 31 August. Amazon moved from 34% lower to 27% lower in July and August. Outside FurHaven, Chewy is now 12% above last year and Amazon 15% below.

What holds. Repeat-purchase lines hold. Pet Factory is level on Amazon and 24% up on Chewy, and Autoship, Chewy’s subscription program, carries 22% of PetWise’s Chewy sales, up from 16% in early 2025. October sales paced above September on both channels (Exhibit 4.78).

What to watch. FurHaven on Amazon was still 41% lower in the latest 31 days of data, and item-level data stop on 27 August (Exhibit 4.82). The number to watch is FurHaven’s weekly units on Chewy against last year.

Ads still earn back less than they cost at each retailer. In October to date ads returned 4.31x at Walmart, 3.30x at Amazon and 3.26x at Chewy, or 35%, 72% and 58% of breakeven (Exhibit 7.10). Breakeven is the return at which ad-attributed sales pay for the ad after product cost and allowances, so it is a floor on direct return, before sales the ads lift elsewhere. On Amazon, the months with higher spend in 2026 brought lower returns: $153K at 4.77x in April, and $359K at 2.66x in September.

Chewy is growing again outside FurHaven, led by repeat-purchase lines.

Excluding FurHaven, Chewy shelf sales were 20% below last year in the first quarter, 12% below in the second and 12% above in the nine weeks to 31 August. Pet Factory chews grew 24% over the year to date, Kitty Sift 77% and goDog, with its new Tiger Tough line, 14%.

What holds. Autoship, which is Chewy’s subscription program, rose from 16% of PetWise’s Chewy sales in early 2025 to 22% this summer. Pet Factory and Kitty Sift sell more than half of their Chewy volume that way. Chewy’s weekly reports show sales up a further 26% between mid-August and mid-October, a seasonal rise led by FurHaven (Exhibit 4.79).

What to watch. FurHaven is half of Chewy sales and was still 28% below last year in the latest nine weeks. Two newer lines, Tiger Tough and Treatly, leave Chewy a margin of about 2%, as thin as the margin it earns on FurHaven.

PetWise shrank on both retailers while their pet categories grew.

Amazon’s pet category grew about 33% in the year to July 2026 and Chewy’s hardgoods about 14% in its latest quarter, while pet supplies sold online grew about 12% in 2025. PetWise’s shelf sales fell 31% on Amazon and 25% on Chewy over 2026 to date. The gap is share lost to other sellers, not a shrinking market.

What holds. The categories are growing where PetWise already has brands: cat products on Amazon grew about three times as fast as dog products, and Chewy says enrichment toys lead its hardgoods growth.

What to watch. The benchmarks cover different periods and measures, so they show direction and not an exact gap. Management reads Amazon hardgoods as falling and gives no source; if that holds for beds, the share loss is smaller than shown here.

The way forward is profit first, on the items that carry the sales.

A few hundred items carry online sales: 257 Amazon items make 81% of its shelf sales and 203 Chewy items make 76%. The plan fixes price, stock, listings and ad returns on those items before it funds growth. It leads with Chewy, where repeat-purchase lines are growing, and runs Amazon for profit. Five levers act mainly online and carry $4.8M of run-rate EBITDA at plan, or about $3.6M weighted for risk.

What holds. The first moves need decisions, not new systems: relist five SmartyKat listings, stop ads on 73 items under 60% of breakeven, hold ad budget on brands filled under 60% and adopt six profit rules (Exhibit 7.22). The plan’s revenue bridge adds $12.5M of online gross sales by 2028 from Chewy, the Amazon recovery and the FurHaven reset (Exhibit 10.17).

What to watch. Retailers set shelf prices, so the FurHaven reset has to be agreed item by item. The head of e-commerce, who owns four of the five levers, is not yet hired. Thirteen weekly measures show whether the fixes hold (Exhibit 10.27), and the number to watch is Chewy shelf sales against last year, which the plan needs level by mid-2027. Item-level marketplace data run to late August 2026 (Exhibit 4.86).

Most first actions are due by March, ahead of the June gate. Wave one starts in December: the cut list, ad budgets tied to stock, the profit rules and the item ceiling. The FurHaven terms reset and the allowance moves follow by March 2027, and about 2,250 small listings are retired or moved by June. Gate one in June 2027 tests monthly breakeven for the company, with Chewy level with last year and ads at breakeven on funded items by mid-2027.

A few hundred items carry most of the online business.

Over the last year, 257 Amazon items sold $25K or more each and made 81% of Amazon shelf sales. On Chewy, 203 items made 76%. At the other end, 1,367 Amazon items and 884 Chewy items sold under $5K each and together made 5% to 6% of sales.

What holds. The hero list is short enough to manage item by item: price, stock, content and retailer margin can be checked weekly for each one.

What to watch. The tail still needs listings kept current, stock held and questions answered. Retiring it frees that effort for the heroes, though each exit should be checked for covers and refills that support a hero item.

Part 05 · Stores

Stores still carry most of PetWise’s sales, and Walmart is the largest of them.

This part covers the store accounts: how large they are, which ones are shrinking, what Walmart’s own sales data shows this autumn, who holds the shelf, and what a change per store is worth.

Stores still carry most of the sales, and retailers’ own brands are taking the shelf.

Store accounts buy about 70% of what PetWise sells, and they have shrunk by about a quarter since 2023. Walmart alone is 38% of store sales. The main rival on the store shelf is the retailer itself: own brands hold more than half of beds and carriers. And the tide is out: across the industry PetWise’s categories shrank about 5% in stores last year while they grew online.

Walmart’s own numbers now show what shoppers bought. Over the past year they spent $97.3M at the shelf on PetWise brands, 2% less than the year before: a little less in stores and a lot more online.

The trouble is in one brand. SmartyKat is down 15% over the latest thirteen weeks while FurHaven and the dog toys are up. The 2027 line reviews decide more of this volume than any online action will.

Sources: PetWise operating plans and margin files; Nielsen store scan data to August 2024; Walmart brand sales channel update, 9 Nov 2026.

Store accounts carry about 70% of PetWise sales and have shrunk each year.

Store accounts bought $117.3M of PetWise’s $166.5M of gross sales in FY25, and the 2026 forecast puts them at $113.7M. They stood at $151.0M in 2023, so the forecast is 25% lower. Online sales fell faster, by 48% between 2023 and FY25, so stores became a larger share of a smaller business.

What holds. Store accounts cost far less to serve in allowances. Discounts and allowances took 9.0% of gross sales in stores in FY25, against 31.3% online.

What to watch. Store shipments fell from $12.6M in March to $6.6M in May 2026 (Exhibit 5.17). Management puts this down to Walmart bedding orders pulled into the first quarter and sold down before the July shelf reset. Monthly figures by account after May were not available, so the second half of 2026 rests on the 5+7 forecast. To September, store sales outside the Costco program ran about 13% below last year (Exhibit 2.02).

On PetWise’s own mix, its categories shrank about 5% in stores last year. Weight NielsenIQ’s category growth by what each PetWise brand sells in stores and online. On that mix its categories shrank about 5% in stores in 2025 and grew about 13% online. PetWise makes about 71% of its sales in stores, so the tide runs against most of what it sells. Walmart’s own data agrees: store sales of PetWise brands there fell 4.3% over the past year. The trade body’s own outlook is for store counts to shrink over the next three years and for online to pass half of pet sales in 2028.

Last year’s store trend would cost slightly more than the plan allows. The plan allows $2.5M of category erosion by the end of 2028, which it reads as about 3% a year on the whole base. Store sales are the part that erodes. At 71% of sales in stores and last year’s fall of about 5%, erosion comes to about $3.0M, about $0.5M more than the allowance. Put the other way, the allowance equals a store trend of about 4.2% a year. The simulator opens on last year’s trend and shows what a faster store decline, or moving more sales online, would do.

Walmart carries 38% of store sales, and most other accounts have shrunk.

Walmart bought $44.9M in FY25, more than the next four store accounts together. Seven of the other eight large accounts were smaller in FY25 than in 2023. Target fell 72% after it moved pet products to its own brand, and Costco fell because its one yearly program moved from late 2025 into early 2026.

What holds. Walmart has stayed within 6% of its 2023 level, and PetSmart grew 9% as it added FurHaven bedding.

What to watch. Walmart reduced scratcher and bedding space in the 2026 plan and reset its pet shelf in July 2026, and what PetWise won or lost at that reset is not in the materials provided. The 2026 forecast names Topco, Petco, Pet Supplies Plus and Target as the largest declines against last year. The 2027 line reviews decide next year’s space, and management ranks them as its first priority.

At Walmart, SmartyKat is losing ground while FurHaven and the dog toys gain.

Walmart’s weekly brand report shows what shoppers paid at the shelf. In the 52 weeks to 9 November they spent $97.3M on PetWise brands, 2.3% less than the year before. Store sales fell 4.3% and Walmart.com, pickup and delivery grew 22.4% to $9.2M, about a tenth of the total.

What holds. FurHaven is up 6.5% over the latest thirteen weeks and goDog and TrustyPup together are up about 6%, so beds and dog toys came through the summer shelf reset well.

What to watch. SmartyKat is half of PetWise’s Walmart sales. It is down 15.3% over the latest thirteen weeks, about $1.9M at the shelf, and its share of Walmart.com search fell in October. The number to watch is SmartyKat’s weekly sales against last year going into the 2027 cat line review.

Walmart shoppers bought slightly less in stores and far more online. Online is still small, about 9% of what Walmart shoppers spend on PetWise brands, but it is where the growth is. Store sales of the same brands fell about $4.0M over the year. Walmart as a whole grew its US online sales 23% in the quarter to October, and PetWise has 43 new items in the pipeline for Walmart’s own online buying.

Retailer own brands hold more than half the store shelf in beds and carriers.

Store scan data for January to August 2024 gives retailer own brands 61% of pet bedding sold in stores and 52% of carriers. They hold 40% of cat products and 23% of dog toys. At Walmart and in the pet specialty chains the own-brand share of bedding is above 80%.

What holds. Dog toys are the one category where own brands lost share, from 24.9% in 2022 to 23.1%. Branded dog toys still have room on the shelf.

What to watch. These shares are the oldest evidence in the packet. They stop on 10 August 2024, before Target, Petco and Walmart changed their pet shelves again. Walmart’s own-brand bedding share includes Vibrant Life beds that PetWise makes, at an estimated 18% of the category (Exhibit 5.18).

PetWise brands lead the branded shelf in carriers and in Walmart cat products. Sherpa held 37% of carrier sales in the pet specialty chains in 2023, SmartyKat 32% of cat products at Walmart and TrustyPup 21% of carriers at Walmart. In each case the retailer’s own brand takes most of the rest, so no other brand can be larger. Five of the eight positions measured lost share between 2022 and August 2024, and the three carrier positions lost the most.

Retailers moving shelf space to their own brands explain the largest store losses.

Target moved its pet range to its own brand in 2024, and PetWise’s sales there fell from $7.9M in 2023 to $2.2M in FY25. At Walmart, the own brand’s share of carriers rose from 28% to 77% within a year as it replaced the branded leader, and TrustyPup’s share slipped from 23% to 18%. Petco has said it uses own brands to fill gaps left by national suppliers.

What holds. Retailers still add brands that bring something their own label lacks. FurHaven grew from under 1% to 13% of Walmart’s bed sales between 2022 and August 2024, beside Vibrant Life, and PetSmart added FurHaven bedding.

What to watch. Target’s own brand took a further $1.5M of dog toys in 2026, Walmart reduced scratcher and bedding space, and Petco is moving space to its own brands. Owned and exclusive brands reached 30.4% of Tractor Supply’s sales. Each range review is a point where space can move, and Petco reviews each quarter.

Own-brand lines outside Topco earn about half the usual store margin.

PetWise also makes product that retailers sell under their own names. Outside Topco, these lines sold $8.8M in the year to June 2025 and earned a 9.0% gross margin, against 17.0% across store accounts. Vibrant Life beds for Walmart earned 11.9% in FY25, and Dentley’s chews for PetSmart 0.5%.

What holds. Topco, the grocery group PetWise supplies with own-brand chews, earned 26.9% over the same period, above the 25% target PetWise set for store accounts. Own-brand supply pays where the terms are right.

What to watch. Vibrant Life sits beside FurHaven on Walmart’s bed shelf, so PetWise supplies its own lowest-priced rival there. Vibrant Life sales fell from $6.7M in 2024 to $3.7M in FY25. The plan sets a 15% margin floor for retailer brands (Exhibit 7.20).

PetWise sells less than $200 a week per store at its largest accounts.

Dividing each account’s FY25 purchases by its store count gives PetWise about $187 a week per Walmart store, $153 at Petco, $124 at Pet Supplies Plus and $114 at PetSmart. Target and Tractor Supply buy about $20 a week per store. These are PetWise’s invoice prices, so shoppers spend more than this at the till.

What holds. Small moves per store are worth a lot. Each $10 a week per Walmart store is about $2.4M a year. goDog reached 1,100 Walmart stores in 2025, about a quarter of the chain.

What to watch. The figure spreads sales over every store, including stores that carry little or no PetWise product, and it includes what each retailer sells online from the same orders. Stores selling each item and sales per store per week by item would tell lost distribution from slower selling. That is the main request of the store scan data (Exhibit 5.28).

A small change in weekly sales per store moves millions of dollars a year. The simulator multiplies a change in weekly sales per store by the number of stores and by 52 weeks. Walmart has about 4,606 stores and the three pet specialty chains about 3,702. It opens on today, with no change. The cases show what the autumn trend at Walmart costs if it runs for a year, and what winning or losing a line review is worth.

KONG leads branded dog toys in stores, where goDog ranks seventeenth.

KONG held 13.7% of dog toys sold in stores in 2023, about twelve times goDog’s 1.1%. Nylabone, Multipet and Chuckit! each held about 5% to 6%. goDog’s store sales fell 14% that year, and 25% in the pet specialty chains.

What to watch. Outside dog toys the assessment names few branded rivals in stores, because own brands take most of the shelf. The online-native sellers in Market and competition are not among the leading store brands recorded here. Current scan data would show whether they have reached the shelf since.

Part 06 · The plan

Fifteen levers add about $26.2M a year before headwinds and risk.

This part sets out what PetWise will do: the six strategic choices, the fifteen initiatives and what each is worth, the order they land in, who carries them and what they cost.

The levers PetWise controls take it most of the way to its target.

The plan is fifteen initiatives in three groups. Commercial levers fix price, trade terms, advertising and the cat range. Operations levers cut the item count, sourcing cost, sites and plant labour. Technology levers lower overhead and rebuild the catalog. Together they are worth about $26.2M a year at full value.

The story in 6 pictures · each opens its detail
Strategy Six choices set where PetWise plays and how it wins.
6choices · whom to serve, which categories, which channels, how to win, what it takes, what to stop
Detail · StrategyLevers Commercial and operations levers each carry about half of the value.

2027 program cash, $MDetail · Funding

Not all of it will land. Weighted for confidence, and after about $7.0M of headwinds, 2028 EBITDA comes to about $6.2M. That is a swing of about $12.9M from this year’s loss, and it is earned on flat sales: the plan makes more on what PetWise already sells.

It still leaves about $3.8M to find. That has to come from the 2027 launches and from delivering more of each lever than the weights assume, which is what the last part of this packet tests.

Sources: Advisor model; PetWise operating plans and board decks.

The strategy is to win where owners still spend and fix what PetWise controls.

Owners are protecting routine care and trimming discretionary pet spending, cat ownership is growing faster than dog ownership, and pet supplies are moving online. PetWise holds brands in the growing parts of that market but is priced above rivals in beds, short of stock online and carrying a cost base built for higher sales. The strategy makes six choices from that evidence, and the fifteen initiatives carry them out.

What holds. More than half of the value sits in trade terms, items, sourcing and landed cost, plants and sites, which PetWise can change without waiting for a retailer.

What to watch. The growth choices depend on retailers and line reviews. At half of plan, cat growth, the FurHaven reset and key-account programs would remove about $2.9M from the full-potential case.

The initiatives sit in three pillars and carry those choices. The 2026 business loses about $6.7M before the one-time tariff refunds. Fifteen initiatives in three pillars take EBITDA most of the way to the target, and most of the gain comes from margin and cost, so the outcome depends more on execution than on the market.

Commercial and operations levers each deliver about half of the gain.

The bridge starts from the 2026 underlying loss and adds $26.2M of levers at plan, pillar by pillar. Headwinds of $7.0M, including about $1M a year of retailer tariff give-backs, are shown separately so that the gains are not netted against them. The full-potential end point is about $12M, and risk weighting brings it to about $5.9M of run-rate by late 2028. A launch reserve of about $5M of plan value, counted at low confidence until each launch is sized, adds about $2.5M, and ten more points of capture on every lever would cover the rest of the gap to $10M.

What holds. Each lever is sized from PetWise’s own FY25 and 2026 data, then checked against published benchmarks.

What to watch. The bridge assumes reinvestment of about $2M a year in talent and tools. Cutting it would raise EBITDA on paper but slow the levers that depend on it.

Assumption · risk weighting

High, medium and low-confidence levers count at 90%, 70% and 50% of plan. That brings the full-potential $12M to about $5.9M of run-rate by late 2028. Reaching $10M without the reserve needs about 90% of plan value, against an average weight of 75%. The reserve counts at 50% because items first sold since July 2025 made about 5% of this year’s Amazon and Chewy shelf sales (Exhibit 4.84; A-03, A-37, A-56).

Note · what is excluded

The plan contains no acquisitions or disposals. Every lever is an operating change inside PetWise.

Three waves carry the plan case past the target late next year.

Wave one is a 90-day sprint on terms, prices, ads, items and overhead, and it includes relisting the dark cat items. Wave two builds capabilities in planning, sourcing, plants and Chewy and resets FurHaven’s shelf prices, and wave three carries the growth moves. Risk-adjusted, the run-rate peaks at about $6.4M in mid-2028, so the launch reserve and faster delivery have to close the gap to $10M.

What holds. About $7.9M of run-rate comes from wave-one actions that need no new systems or sites, and each wave helps fund the next.

What to watch. Wave three depends on 2027 line reviews at Walmart and pet specialty, which PetWise does not control. A late Mundelein decision moves about $1M of 2027 savings into 2028.

The waves overlap, so quick wins help fund the later moves. The timeline shows each initiative from launch to full run-rate value, with a dot where half of its value is reached. Wave-one actions start inside the first 90 days, the capability builds run through 2027, and the growth moves follow the 2027 line reviews.

Operations lead the ramp, and dated milestones give a monthly read on progress.

Operations levers reach about $11M of run-rate by the end of 2027 because items, sourcing, plants and sites are within PetWise’s control. Commercial levers reach about $10M by then and keep building as cat and account programs mature. Thirteen milestones and three gates track the ramp: monthly breakeven by June 2027, a run-rate of about $8M by December 2027 and about $10M by June 2028. The base case reaches breakeven a quarter late, about $5.1M by December 2027 and about $6.4M at the third gate, so the gates also test whether the launch reserve has been found.

What holds. Wave-one actions in both pillars start inside the first 90 days, and each milestone has an owner and a date the board can check.

What to watch. Commercial growth depends on 2027 line reviews and retailer terms, so its ramp carries more risk than the cost levers. If gate one is missed, the plan pulls forward the next wave of cost actions rather than waiting for growth, and if the launch reserve is not sized by then, the 2028 target needs resetting.

Dated milestones give the board a monthly read on progress. The timeline covers the first fourteen months of the plan. Most decisions fall before February 2027, and the first two stage gates follow in mid-2027 and at the end of 2027.

The plan needs a few senior hires and a smaller, sharper team.

Six roles carry most of the new work: a head of e-commerce, a revenue management lead, a data and AI product lead, two planners and a sourcing engineer in Asia. Together with platforms and content they cost about $2M a year. A small value office, led by a senior operator, tracks every initiative weekly.

What holds. The roles pay back through levers worth far more than their cost.

What to watch. Hiring takes time, so interim specialists should start the revenue management and e-commerce work in December.

Freed inventory covers the one-off costs, but not the product transitions.

Cutting to about 1,500 items and 120 days of supply releases about $7–8M of inventory cash in 2027: about $6M from buying less core stock and about $1.7M from selling excess and obsolete stock at about 20% of cost. One-off costs, including severance, moves, stranded lease and technology projects, are about $4.5M. Management also estimates about $15M of cash for product transitions, markdowns and retailer price changes, needed by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

What holds. The levers and one-off costs alone net to about +$3M of cash in 2027.

What to watch. The product-transition need is not yet sized line by line, and part of it may be launch inventory already in the buying plan. Cash closed September at $11.0M, and the 13-week view has a low of $7.2M on 6 November and $12.1M on 8 January, with no refund assumed. Until the transitions are sized, the launches should be phased against cash and the planning-platform and ERP spend should follow the first quarter.

Part 07 · Commercial

The commercial levers add about $12M at plan, led by trade terms and cat.

This part takes the commercial levers one at a time: trade terms, cat growth, Chewy and the marketplaces, the digital shelf, advertising, the FurHaven reset and the key accounts.

Commercial value starts with terms and price, ahead of new products.

Seven commercial levers are worth about $12M a year at plan. The largest is plain. PetWise pays retailers allowances worth about a third of online sales and about 9% in stores, and the rate varies widely from one account to the next. Spending that money where it earns placement is worth about $3M.

The story in 6 pictures · each opens its detail
Terms Allowances vary widely from one account to the next.
Allowances as a share of gross sales, by accountDetail · Revenue managementCat Cat sales are slipping before the new range arrives.
Cat category sales to September, $MDetail · Cat growthChewy Chewy’s gap to last year has narrowed each quarter.
Chewy weekly sales against last yearDetail · Chewy and marketplacesAds Ads return less than breakeven at each of the three retailers.
Return on ad spend against breakevenDetail · Retail mediaFurHaven Reversing shelf-price rises is worth more than a new value tier.
Gross sales won back by 2028, $MDetail · FurHaven resetAccounts Several accounts earn too little to justify their cost to serve.
Gross margin by accountDetail · Key accounts

Cat is the growth engine: the best margins in the portfolio, in the species that is growing. FurHaven needs its price reset before anything new. Advertising returns less than it costs at each of the three retailers, and a named list of 73 items covers most of the fix.

The latest numbers sharpen three of these. Ad spend is up by more than a third this year while the sales it brings are down, so the ad rule matters more. Chewy is now selling FurHaven beds below its own cost, so the price reset has to be agreed before the retailer forces it. And cat owners are spending more while SmartyKat sells less, so the cat range has to be back on the shelf before it can grow.

Sources: PetWise margin files and board decks; PetWise paid media dashboard; PetWise e-commerce war room, 13 Nov 2026.

Allowances are PetWise’s largest controllable commercial cost.

Discounts and allowances took $25.5M, or 15% of FY25 gross sales. They ran at 31% of gross on e-commerce against 9% in stores, and above 40% at Costco. Revenue growth management, which means managing price, promotion, pack and trade terms together, targets about $3M.

What holds. McKinsey reports that disciplined pricing and promotion work lifts trade-spend effectiveness by 10% to 20%. The plan assumes about 6%, below that range. Management already plans a trade-promotion tool and accrual-based trade accounting for 2027, which is the core of this lever. The marketplace data shows where to start: before allowances, Amazon earns 44% to 49% on Sherpa and goDog, and Chewy about 4% on FurHaven.

What to watch. Retailers will resist, and several now want part of the tariff refund back. The plan trades allowance cuts and concessions for in-stock, forecast-accuracy and placement commitments rather than conceding them outright. October e-commerce promotions and deductions cost about $690K of cash, and sell-through deductions take 90–120 days to pay back.

Note · what counts as allowances

Allowances are all discounts and allowances booked against gross sales: retailer programs, co-op, damages, deductions and promotional funding.

Assumption · size of the prize

About 6% better use of about $25M of allowances gives about $1.5M. Recovering invalid deductions adds about $0.6M and price and mix about $0.9M, for about $3.0M in all (A-07, A-08).

Retailers want part of the tariff refund back, which pulls against the terms reset. After the IEEPA tariffs fell, Topco, Petco, PetSmart, Tractor Supply and Walmart each asked for money, price or terms. The one-time asks offset the refund, and the plan carries the recurring cost-price cuts as a headwind of about $1M a year. PetWise’s own Topco analysis shows the surcharge recovered real costs: after non-refunded duty, freight and materials it is about $92K ahead over 15 months.
