Cat brands earn the best margins in the portfolio and serve the growing species.

SmartyKat and Kitty Sift sold about $43M in FY25 at 23% to 32% gross margin, against 20% for FurHaven and 10% for Pet Factory. The cat brands need restoring before they grow: SmartyKat’s Amazon sales halved in 2026, five listings that went dark explain about 80% of that fall, and the five cat categories ran about 11% below last year to September. From about $38M in 2026 the plan grows cat sales about 11% a year to about $47M in 2028, carried by management’s 2027 slate: SmartyKat+ at PetSmart from April 2027, ten electronic toys, a Complete Needs Home set for Walmart and freeze-dried cat treats for Walmart and Petco.

What holds. Demand is intact where the product is on the shelf. Hot Pursuit grew 56% on Amazon, a silvervine catnip item more than doubled on Chewy and Kitty Sift grew 77% on Chewy.

What to watch. Walmart is the largest cat customer, so the 2027 line review decides most of this lever. Kitty Sift fell 21% on Amazon, and the gap widened over the summer.

Cat sales are falling before the 2027 slate arrives. Cat toys, scratchers, litter and cat furniture each sold less to September, and catnip alone grew. The 2027 slate is what has to turn this round, and none of its launches yet carries a sales or margin target.

Cat owners are spending more while SmartyKat is selling less.

The demand side of the cat lever has strengthened. Cats outnumber dogs, more homes keep several, and products are the largest part of what a cat owner spends, about 39%. 81% of Gen Z cat owners and 71% of men who own cats bought toys last year. SmartyKat is moving the other way: down 15% at Walmart over thirteen weeks, down 33% on Amazon in October and 48% below its October forecast. Two findings in the survey bear on the 2027 range. Pet superstores and online retailers now rival mass stores for cat toys, and SmartyKat sells mostly through Walmart. And younger owners are buying cheaper gifts, about $25 each against $42 a year before, which favours a range with entry prices.

Chewy has stabilised and is growing again outside FurHaven.

Chewy shelf sales ran about a quarter below last year over the first 35 weeks of 2026, but the gap narrowed from 31% in the first quarter to 11% in the third quarter to date. Outside FurHaven, sales were 12% above last year in the latest nine weeks. The plan adds about $3.2M of Chewy sales at PetWise’s prices by 2028, and about $1M through the Walmart.com and Target.com seller accounts.

What holds. Autoship, Chewy’s subscription program, now carries 22% of PetWise’s Chewy sales, up from 16% in early 2025. Chews and litter sell more than half of their Chewy volume that way. Stock was the brake: Amazon cut $5.6M and Chewy $3.5M of PetWise orders to September, and fill rate passed 85% in October.

What to watch. The seller accounts on Walmart.com and Target.com sell under $1M a year between them, and Walmart.com fell 22% from April to October. Management is moving the Walmart.com seller items to Walmart’s own buying, with more than 350 items planned, so the larger Walmart.com opportunity sits with the Walmart buying team and the seller accounts stay a capped test. Chewy is also building its own brands toward the low-to-mid teens of sales.

Fewer, stronger listings sell far more per listing than a sprawling catalog.

FurHaven sold about $3K per Amazon dog-bed listing across 977 listings, against $21K for Bedsure and $58K for KSIIA. Across the brands, 257 items made 81% of PetWise’s Amazon sales over the last year, while 1,367 items made 5%. About a fifth of Amazon traffic to PetWise is organic, and 98% of organic bedding searches are unbranded.

What holds. Pet Factory and Kitty Sift convert well above the portfolio average, which shows that complete, review-rich listings sell.

What to watch. Cutting listings removes some sales in the short run. The plan exits the long tail or moves it to a seller account rather than keeping it on vendor terms.

AI recommendations already sway a large minority of shoppers.

40% of US shoppers say an AI recommendation has influenced something they bought, close to the share who say the same of influencers. Amazon says more than 400 million customers used its shopping assistant in the past year and that they spend about 50% more per order. An assistant shows a shopper two or three items, not a page of forty, and it picks them from ratings, reviews and complete product data. Amazon’s October figures show what losing that choice costs: more views and fewer buyers (Exhibit 4.29). The digital-shelf lever is the plan’s answer, and its measure is hero listings rated 4.3 or higher with full content.

Paid media runs below breakeven at Walmart, Amazon and Chewy.

In October to date ads returned 4.31x at Walmart, 3.30x at Amazon and 3.26x at Chewy, against breakevens of about 12.2x, 4.6x and 5.6x on realized prices. In September about $637K of ad spend earned back about $352K of contribution, a shortfall of about $284K a month before any lift to unadvertised sales. Amazon search returns fell from 4.77x in April to 2.05x in September as cost per click rose from $0.88 to $2.22, and October’s fixes lifted them to 2.78x on flat spend.

What holds. The first cuts are named. 73 items running under 60% of breakeven took about $232K of spend and returned about $148K less contribution than they cost. Stopping them is worth about $0.9M a year against the lever’s $1.0M, and 89 items clear breakeven and can take more budget.

What to watch. Breakeven counts ad-attributed sales and leaves out the lift ads give to other sales, so the shortfall is a floor on direct return and not a loss figure. The item lists use margins and sales to mid-July, before October’s Amazon changes, so they need re-running on current data before budgets move. Management’s plan adds online video, connected TV, influencers and paid TikTok, and performance marketing ran 69% above last year to September, so new channels need hold-out tests before they scale.

Stopping the named cut list delivers most of the lever. On October’s pace the three retailers spend about $730K a month on ads and earn back about $449K of contribution, a shortfall of about $281K a month. Stopping the cut list recovers about $72K of that a month, or about $0.9M a year against the lever’s $1.0M, and returns about 3% higher on the remaining spend deliver the rest. Direct breakeven is further off. With nothing else changed it needs returns about 63% higher, and the top of the range, Walmart and Amazon back at their 2025 returns, is 44% higher. The year-end plan spends about 10% more at slightly lower returns, which widens the shortfall to about $324K a month.

Ad spend rose sharply over twelve weeks while the sales it brought fell. Over the twelve weeks to 14 November PetWise spent $1.6M on sponsored ads at the three retailers, $0.6M more than a year before, and the sales those ads brought were $0.4M lower. Each $1 of ads returned $3.22 against $5.84. More of the clicks became orders, but each click cost $1.30 against $0.74 and the average order fell from $22.48 to $18.13. For the year to date spend is up 36%, about $1.2M, for 7% less in ad-attributed sales. That extra spend is larger than the whole retail media lever, so the lever looks conservative. The breakeven rule is the decision that releases it.

FurHaven’s recovery starts with shelf prices, ahead of new products.

Shelf prices on the same FurHaven items rose about 7% on Chewy and 5% on Amazon in a year, while PetWise’s own prices moved about 1%. Items priced up more than 10% lost about 60% of their units. Chewy earned about 4% on FurHaven before allowances, so it had reason to raise prices. The plan resets terms on the affected items so that last year’s shelf prices pay the retailer, then adds a value tier at $30 to $60. Management is relaunching the brand as FurHaven+ for pet specialty in January 2027, FurHaven for mass retail in March and PopHaven for impulse, with price enforcement live by April, so the first step is to set each tier’s price and the enforced price against the $45–65 band before launch.

What holds. On Chewy, FurHaven items whose shelf price held lost about 6% of their units, and items cut in price by more than 10% grew 4%. The reset moves money from allowances into the invoice price, so PetWise’s net price need not fall.

What to watch. Retailers set shelf prices, so the reset has to be agreed item by item and tested on the twenty largest items first. On Amazon, flat-priced FurHaven items still lost 44% of their units, so price alone will not restore traffic there.

Beds lost most where shelf prices rose and held at Walmart. Beds lost $11.8M to September, 31% of last year’s sales. Amazon and Chewy took most of the loss, while Walmart, where FurHaven sells at its lowest prices, grew 6%. That fits a loss led by shelf price and listings rather than by the category.

The reset pays as long as the sales won back outweigh what PetWise gives up. The plan counts about $4.0M of FurHaven sales won back by 2028 at about 30% contribution, worth $1.2M, or about $0.8M weighted for risk. It assumes retailers fund lower shelf prices from their own margin. That is now in doubt: about 26% of FurHaven’s October sales on Chewy were below Chewy’s cost. The simulator shows what happens if PetWise has to give up invoice price to fund the reset.

Several accounts earn too little margin to justify their cost to serve.

Walmart, Topco, Chewy, Amazon, Petco and PetSmart earn 20% to 24% gross margin. Pet Supplies Plus, Tractor Supply and WinCo earn under 7%, and the FY25 Costco program lost money. Each low-margin account gets a repricing offer, a different assortment or an exit.

What holds. The 2026 Costco program was repriced and earns about 41% product margin, so club programs can work on the right terms. Costco bought $11.2M of goDog toys to September against $1.5M a year before, though the 2027 program is not yet confirmed.

What to watch. Exiting accounts and lines removes about $8M of gross sales in 2027, which the plan replaces with cat growth, Chewy and the FurHaven recovery.

Part 08 · Operations

The operations levers add about $12M at plan, starting with the item count.

This part takes the operations levers one at a time: the item count, sourcing, sites, plants, duty and freight, inventory and service.

Operations add about $12M by making and moving fewer things, better.

Six operations levers are worth about $12.4M at plan, and they are the most certain part of it because they rest on PetWise’s own decisions. Cut the catalog to about 1,500 items. Re-quote the largest product spend. Run fewer, fuller sites. Bring plant labour down to targets management has already set. Lock in duty and freight. Plan stock with better forecasts.

The evidence since the summer is encouraging. The item cut has started: the October item list flags 1,013 of 2,511 online items as discontinued. Fill rates are up sharply on both Amazon and Chewy.

Three things cut the other way. Ocean freight is about three times last autumn’s level. The 2027 range adds several hundred items with no exits shown. And the margin on online shipments is running below the forecast, which may be mix or may be duty and freight reaching product cost.

Sources: PetWise operating reviews; PetWise monthly business review workbook, October 2026; PetWise weekly e-commerce report, week ended 14 Nov 2026; Drewry World Container Index, 12 Nov 2026.

Cutting to about 1,500 active items removes most of the loss-making tail.

PetWise sold 5,423 items in FY25, and 837 of them lost $5.3M of gross margin. Discontinued items still cost $1.5M. Cutting to about 1,500 active items and repricing the remaining loss-makers targets about $2M.

What holds. L.E.K. finds that SKU rationalisation adds 65 to 90 bps of gross margin, and McKinsey cites a case where a 25% cut lifted gross margin by 2 to 4 points.

What to watch. Cuts must follow contribution after allowances and freight, not sales rank, or good small items go with the bad. Management’s 2027 slate adds several hundred items, with more sizes and online-only colours, and shows no exits, so the item ceiling has to net launches against exits. Each 250 items kept costs about $0.2M of the saving.

Each few hundred items kept or added takes savings out of the plan. The item lever is worth about $2.0M at a ceiling of about 1,500 active items, and each 250 items above that costs about $0.2M. The cut is under way: 1,013 online items are flagged discontinued, and 630 Amazon items that sold under $500 in October made 4% of its sales. The simulator shows what happens if the cut stalls, or if the 2027 launches are added without matching exits.

Should-cost sourcing and redesign can take about 2.5% out of product cost.

Product cost was about $103M in FY25, bought from a fragmented supplier base. Re-quoting top items against should-cost models, consolidating suppliers and redesigning beds and packaging targets about $2.5M. BCG and Inverto put AI-assisted savings at up to 5% of direct spend.

What holds. Management’s own work found real examples: the Nest Top sofa bed’s margin rose from 28% to 35% on a redesigned bill of materials, and foam specifications can fall 12%.

What to watch. Supplier changes take two to three production cycles to land, so savings start in mid-2027. Management won committed-item discounts of 3–7% over the summer and is setting up a China sourcing entity by March 2027, but product cost still ran about $1.2M worse than forecast to September once the larger refund is set aside, as non-refunded duty and freight rose.

Fewer, fuller sites can save about $3M a year.

PetWise ran ten US sites in May 2026, with about $7M of annual leases. Exiting Mundelein manufacturing and folding the El Paso warehouse into Wilmer target about $2.4M. Management judges a McAllen consolidation not feasible and will renew on a 3-year term with two 5-year options, so McAllen is out of the lever. Central Garden & Pet has closed 13 facilities since 2022 on the same logic.

What holds. Wilmer has about 55K of its 150K square feet unused, so it can absorb volume without new space.

What to watch. The Mundelein lease runs to December 2028, so the exit date and sublet terms decide the savings. Pet Factory chews sell about $6M a year on Amazon at shelf prices and are growing on Chewy, so supply has to hold through the move. Management is bringing on Santa Fe, the rawhide partner described in May as in distress, as a finished-goods supplier by March 2027 and plans one manufacturing hub by June 2027. The new Chip Dips collagen chews carry a US-made flag, so where they are made after the exit needs settling first.

Plant labour can fall to the levels management has already targeted.

Plant labour ran at about 15.5% of sales at Corry, 16% at McAllen and 18% at Mundelein in 2025. Management’s targets are 10%, 11.5% and 15%. Scheduling, standard work and labour analytics target about $2M.

What holds. Corry’s 2026 plan already lowers labour per unit from $2.69 to $1.92, so the method has been tested.

What to watch. Volume must be steady for productivity to hold, which is why planning and item cuts come first.

Duty savings depend on where fabric is made, not where beds are sewn.

PetWise pays about $8M a year in customs duty. A China-origin textile bed pays about 27% against 17% from Cambodia or India, but origin follows the fabric. US assembly pays duty on inputs, and 2027 ocean contracts can lock in rates below the autumn spot level.

What holds. Spot freight from Shanghai to Los Angeles was $7,514 per container on 29 October against $2,442 in January, and BIMCO expects a weaker 2027 market.

What to watch. Non-refunded duty is rising: on Topco items it went from about 4% in early 2025 to about 18% by July 2026 after the Section 122 and 2026 Section 301 tariffs, and the US–China truce runs to 10 January 2027. Management’s ocean consolidation program, running to April 2027, supports the freight part of this lever.

AI-led planning can release cash tied up in slow stock.

Inventory fell from $72M in early 2023 to $41M in January 2026. Excess stock has since fallen from $9.4M to about $5.5–6.0M, with about $2.5M obsolete and about $1M tied up in the Kaifeng dispute, against a $4.6M reserve. Liquidation has recovered only about 20% of cost, so the cash lever is buying less, not selling old stock. Better forecasts, fewer items and weekly planning target 120 days and about $1.5M less margin lost to clearance. McKinsey finds AI forecasting cuts errors by 20% to 50%.

What holds. Item cuts and the planning platform reinforce each other, because fewer items make forecasts easier. Management has already stopped buying long-tail items and is moving buy dollars to top sellers and new items. Forecast accuracy rose 11 points from April to August, and inventory stood at $42.5M in September with 156 days on hand against management’s near-term target of 135.

What to watch. Clearing excess stock costs margin up front, so the write-down should be taken once and early. Of 215 Amazon items that sold almost daily in 2025, 40 now sell on fewer than half of days, so the planning work should start with the hero items.

Chewy fill rate has swung far below the level the plan requires.

Chewy fill rate was 74% in late September 2025 and 86% in late September 2026, after an 80% to 94% swing over the summer. Low stock on key items suppresses Chewy’s search ranking, which compounds the lost sales. Across all accounts PetWise shipped 80.1% of what customers tried to order from January to September 2026. That left about $28.1M of estimated demand unserved, of which store accounts hold $14.5M and Amazon and Chewy $13.4M (Exhibits 4.51 and 4.53).

What holds. Fill rate reached 93.6% in late August 2026, so the target is within reach.

What to watch. Zero-stock items with demand rose from 12 to 30 over the summer, the clearest early warning. On Amazon, PetWise filled 37% to 53% of Sherpa, SmartyKat and goDog orders in September, and stock cover fell from 14 weeks to 8 in a year (Exhibits 4.80 and 4.81).

Holding the autumn fill rates is worth most of the marketplace lever. From January to September Amazon received 64% and Chewy 68% of the demand they placed. Over the latest twelve weeks those figures are 76% and 86%. If half of the unserved demand is real and not repeat orders, holding the autumn levels for a year recovers about $3.8M of sales and about $0.8M of EBITDA. The simulator shows the range.

Part 09 · Technology and AI

AI use cases enable about a third of the value, once the data is fixed.

This part covers what has to be true in data and systems for the levers to work, the AI use cases that carry value, and the order they are built in.

Data comes before technology, because PetWise cannot yet see profit by item.

About a third of the plan’s value depends on software and AI, but none of it works until the basics are fixed. PetWise runs two ERPs, carried current tariffs in the standard cost of about 300 of its 3,300 items this year, and cannot see profit by item after allowances, ads and freight. That gap comes first.

Then four use cases carry most of the value: demand planning, a content factory for listings, ad bidding with hold-out tests, and back-office automation. Most are bought, not built, and pay back within a year.

One thing has moved fast outside. Amazon and Walmart now let AI assistants shop for people, and four in ten shoppers say an AI recommendation has already swayed a purchase. Assistants read listings, reviews and product data, so complete content has become a sales lever, not housekeeping.

Sources: PetWise systems review; advisor model; Amazon and Walmart announcements, 2026.

PetWise cannot yet see profit by item, and that gap comes first.

Standard costs carried current tariffs on about 300 of 3,300+ items in 2026, two ERPs run side by side, and the retailer data carries sales but no stock, fill-rate or advertising figures. Without item-level profit after allowances, ads and freight, pricing, item and ad decisions run on averages. The first 90 days build that view.

What holds. Product content is in good shape: all items were loaded into Salsify by November 2025.

What to watch. Data work rarely wins priority in a squeeze, so the value office should own the data milestones.

Sources: PetWise 5+7 plan notes; e-commerce systems review; Chewy data review (2026).

AI use cases enable about a third of the plan’s gross value.

Ten use cases support the commercial and operations levers, from demand forecasting to deduction recovery. Together they enable about $10M of the $26M gross plan. Most use proven tools rather than custom models.

What holds. The fastest use cases, ad bidding, deductions and content, pay back within a quarter.

What to watch. AI value is counted inside the initiatives it supports, never added on top.

Planning, content, media and the back office are the use cases that carry the value.

Each use case below sits inside a lever that is already in the plan, so none of it is extra value. Planning touches the most levers. The content factory is the fastest to pay back. Media bidding and the back office fund part of the reinvestment.

What holds. Most of the capability is bought or partnered, and a person approves anything that reaches a retailer or a price.

What to watch. Adoption is the risk, not the software. The measure to watch is forecast accuracy on the few hundred hero items.

AI demand planning touches the most levers in the plan.

A planning platform fed by retailer point-of-sale and inventory data sets buys and stock by item and account each week. McKinsey finds AI forecasting cuts errors 20% to 50% and lost sales from stock-outs by up to 65%. The plan targets 120 days of supply, a 95% Chewy fill rate and half the excess and obsolete stock.

What holds. Chewy’s vendor statements already carry days of supply, forecasts and fill rates, so the data exists.

What to watch. Forecasts depend on a clean item master, so the item cut comes first.

Generative AI can rebuild the catalog for AI shopping assistants within months.

Gen-AI tools draft attributes, titles, images and answers from the item master and reviews, and a small team approves them. The plan cuts Amazon to about 300 hero listings, Chewy to about 600 and Walmart to about 400, each complete and review-rich. Agency and content spend falls by about $0.4M.

What holds. McKinsey estimates that gen AI lifts marketing productivity by 5% to 15% of marketing spend.

What to watch. Assistant rankings change often, so the content team should test and refresh monthly.

Machine bidding and hold-out tests can lift ad returns toward breakeven.

Branded Amazon campaigns returned 4.13x against 1.34x for non-branded ones, and nine campaigns returned 0.38x on a quarter of spend. Rules-based bidding with weekly hold-out tests moves budget to what pays. The same elasticity data then sets prices, since a 1% price rise on Chewy cost about 1.9% of units.

What holds. Pacvue is already in place on Amazon and Chewy, so this is a process change more than a tool purchase. The paid media dashboard already sets a breakeven for each item, from about 2.4x to over 25x, so bids can follow item margin (Exhibit 7.31).

What to watch. Cutting branded spend cost share of voice in 2026, so branded defence stays funded.

Automation in the back office funds part of the reinvestment.

One ERP instead of two, AI-assisted order entry and cash application, one e-commerce agency instead of the six that rotated through since 2025, and a smaller headquarters footprint target about $1.5M. Deduction recovery adds about $0.6M inside revenue management.

What holds. Suppliers with structured deduction programs typically recover 30% to 60% of invalid deductions.

What to watch. ERP consolidation is the riskiest IT step, so it runs after the 2026 holiday peak with a parallel run.

What to watch. Each tool needs a named business owner, or adoption stalls after launch.

Part 10 · Odds and decisions

Without the launches, about 3% of simulated outcomes reach the target.

This part tests the plan: three named cases, a simulation of 10,000 runs, a simulator to try your own settings, the risks and their triggers, the scorecard, and the decisions needed by February.

On today’s evidence the plan lands well short of its target.

Run the plan 10,000 times, letting each lever deliver more or less than expected and start on time or late, and the middle outcome for 2028 is about $5.5M. Most runs land between $2.4M and $8.6M. About 3% reach $10M.

Two things lift the odds. The first is the 2027 launches: if they add about $5M of plan value, the chance rises to about 22%. The second is delivery: ten more points of capture on each lever, on top of the launches, takes it to about 48%. Neither is in hand. The launches have no sales or margin targets yet, and this autumn’s new items have sold about $86K on about $110K of advertising. The largest of them sold far less in October than in September.

Timing matters most next year. A plan that runs two quarters late costs far more in 2027 than any single lever falling short. So the asks are about pace: seven decisions by the end of February.

Sources: Advisor model and simulation; PetWise monthly business review workbook, October 2026.

The downside case still earns well above today, and plan delivery clears the target.

The downside case assumes slower delivery, a one-quarter slip on the later waves and a weaker category, and it gives about $2.7M in 2028. The base case gives about $6.2M, and the plan delivered in full gives about $12.7M. The three cases leave out the launch reserve. No single lever moves 2028 EBITDA by more than about $0.7M, so the result rests on delivery across the plan rather than on one bet.

What holds. About 12% of simulated outcomes fall below the downside case, so it is a fair stress case rather than a worst case.

What to watch. A two-quarter slip across the plan costs about $7.8M of 2027 EBITDA and about $1.9M in 2028, so dates matter as much as lever value.

Dates matter as much as lever value. A two-quarter slip across the plan costs about $7.8M of 2027 EBITDA and about $1.9M in 2028. No single lever moves 2028 EBITDA by more than about $0.7M when it moves to its low or high case.

Without a launch reserve, the plan has about a 3% chance of its target.

Ten thousand simulated runs vary lever size, delivery, timing, erosion and the starting point. The middle outcome for 2028 is about $5.5M, and eight in ten runs fall between about $2.4M and $8.6M. The chance of $10M or more in 2028 is about 3%, and the chance of $8M or more is about 16%.

What holds. About 42% of runs reach $6M or more, against a loss of about $6.7M today. A launch reserve of about $5M lifts the chance of $10M to about 22%, and ten more points of capture on top to about 48%.

What to watch. The base case assumes no slips and plan-level erosion, so it sits above the middle of the simulated range: about 62% of runs fall below it in 2028 and about 81% in 2027. The three gates are met on their dates in about 1%, about 3% and about 3% of runs without the reserve. Across the settings tested in Exhibit 10.35 the chance of $10M stays between about 0% and 6%.

A launch reserve and more capture would lift the odds. Each bar changes one thing in the simulation and re-reads the chance of $10M or more in 2028. A launch reserve of about $5M lifts it from about 3% to about 22%, and ten more points of capture on top to about 48%. The reserve is a what-if size and is not plan value: management’s 2027 launches are its candidates, none is sized yet, and items first sold since July 2025 made about 5% of this year’s Amazon and Chewy shelf sales (Exhibit 4.84).

The autumn launches have sold little so far, with heavy advertising behind two.

The launch reserve rests on the 2027 range, so the record of the 2026 launches matters. Since the summer the new items on Amazon and Chewy have sold about $86K in total. Chip Dips and the freeze-dried cat treats each cost more in advertising than they sold. It is early, and stores are not in this data, but it is the reason the reserve counts at low confidence until each launch carries a sales, margin and cash target.

Chip Dips, the largest of the new items, sold far less in October than September.

Chip Dips sold $18.8K across retailers in September and $7.2K in October, a fall of 62% in its fourth month. On Amazon, visits to the listing more than tripled in October and sales fell by about two-thirds. The team reports slipping ratings, a stock-out at Chewy and reviews that mention staining and taste. NielsenIQ’s study of this year’s most successful launches finds four things they had in common: the product was on the shelf, shoppers knew of it, they could try it, and support lasted past the first months. Companies that grow sales from new products are about twice as likely to grow in total. Each 2027 launch should be held to the same four tests before the reserve counts.

The simulator shows what delivery, timing and erosion each do to the result.

The simulator opens on the base case, where 2028 EBITDA is about $6.2M, about $3.8M below the target, and 2027 EBITDA is about breakeven. Without the launch reserve, about 15 more points of delivery on both groups of levers bring 2028 to $10M on the planned dates. Starting waves two and three one quarter late takes about $2.6M from 2027 and about $0.5M from 2028. The three buttons load the cases in Exhibit 10.28.

What holds. The simulator uses the same model, ramps and lever values as the rest of this packet, and each slider stays inside the range the simulation draws from.

What to watch. The chance shown is indicative. It moves the simulated spread in Exhibit 10.03 to the chosen settings rather than re-running the simulation.

Retailer give-backs, the launch reserve and leadership capacity are the largest risks.

The plan asks a lean team to run fifteen initiatives at once while retailers seek part of the tariff refund back and management’s own plan adds items and advertising. The largest risks are the give-backs, finding the launch reserve, thin commercial and e-commerce leadership and the 2027 line reviews. Each risk below has a response and an early warning.

What holds. Even the downside case earns about $2.7M in 2028, against a loss of about $6.7M today, and demand in cat, enrichment and online channels is growing.

What to watch. A simulation puts the chance of $10M or more in 2028 at about 3%. A launch reserve of about $5M lifts it to about 22%, and ten more points of lever capture on top to about 48%. A value office with weekly tracking is the main control on delivery.

Three autumn readings could move next year’s starting line.

Three readings from the autumn bear on where 2027 starts, and none is settled. Each has a size and a piece of evidence that would settle it, so the 2027 budget can carry them on purpose and not by default. The budget should also be built on what shoppers bought this autumn, not on what PetWise shipped.

Ten measures, reviewed monthly, show whether the plan is on track.

The scorecard pairs outcome measures, EBITDA and gross margin, with the drivers that lead them: allowances, items, fill rate, stock, ad returns and sites. Each has a dated gate.

What holds. Most measures exist in PetWise reporting today. The online ones can be read weekly from the marketplace database, and the rest come with the item P&L.

What to watch. If more than three measures miss two months running, the value office escalates to the board. The item-level data behind the online measures run to late August 2026 (Exhibit 4.86).

Margin, availability and trade terms are the measures that prove the plan.

Gross margin shows whether pricing, sourcing and complexity work is landing. Chewy fill rate shows whether planning has fixed availability. E-commerce allowances show whether trade terms have moved.

What holds. Each measure is already reported, or can be built from data PetWise holds today, including weekly sell-through from the marketplace database.

What to watch. E-commerce allowances sit at 31% of gross. If they have not fallen below 28% by mid-2027, the revenue management case needs a reset.

The plan needs seven decisions by the end of February.

The 2027 budget, annual trade terms, the retailers’ tariff give-back asks and two leases fall due between mid-December and the end of January. Each decision below unlocks a wave-one action, and the plan also ends five habits that have worked against margin.

What holds. Each decision has one owner and one date, and each sits with a named executive or the board. Management has already set the brand roles, with a plus brand for pet specialty and a core brand for mass retail.

What to watch. About $15M of product-transition cash is needed by the end of the first quarter of 2027, and the 2027 launches that would form the launch reserve are not yet sized line by line.

The plan also ends five habits that have worked against margin. Each practice below has cost PetWise margin or cash. The value protected overlaps the initiatives that deliver it, so it is not added to the plan total.

Part 11 · Assumptions and method

Each figure in this packet traces to a source and a stated assumption.

Tabs reference assumption identifiers rather than restating them. Where the data is thin, the gap is named and the estimate is marked as ours.

Each figure in the plan traces to a source and an assumption.

This is the register. Each assumption used anywhere in the packet appears here once, with its identifier, the value used, its basis and how much the result moves if it is wrong.

The plan is built from PetWise data and checked against outside benchmarks.

The callouts below state how the packet was built, what it does not do and where the data is thin.

Method · how levers are sized

Each lever is sized from PetWise’s own FY25 item, brand and customer data, the 2026 5+7 plan and the marketplace database, then checked against published benchmarks.

Method · marketplace data

Marketplace figures are what shoppers bought at shelf prices. Year-to-date comparisons use the same days for Amazon and matching weeks for Chewy, and same-item price measures use 2025 units as weights (A-27, A-28, A-30).

Method · scope

The packet covers operating levers only. Every lever is a change PetWise makes in how it sells, makes, moves and runs the business.

Method · risk weighting

High, medium and low-confidence levers count at 90%, 70% and 50% of plan value (A-03). Headwinds and reinvestment are counted in full.

Method · simulation

The simulation runs the plan model 10,000 times with a fixed seed, drawing lever size, capture, timing, erosion, retailer give-backs and the starting point each time. The launch reserve is tested as a what-if on the same draws. The spreads and slip chances are advisor judgements, and Exhibit 10.35 shows the result under different settings (A-32 to A-35).

Method · competitor read

Competitor prices, ratings and rating counts were read from public retailer pages, most on 10 November 2026, one like-for-like hero item per category. Amazon figures are third-party estimates and dog-bed shares are from early 2025 (A-38, A-39).

Method · paid media read

Paid media figures come from PetWise’s paid media dashboard, with data to 26 October 2026. Breakeven is realized price over pre-ad contribution margin per unit, so it counts ad-attributed sales and leaves out halo. The dashboard’s source files were not read for this packet (A-43 to A-46).

Method · store read

Store-account sales and margins come from PetWise’s operating plans and margin files, at invoice prices. Brand shares on the store shelf come from store scan data for 2022 to 10 August 2024, in retail dollars, and retailer positions from their published results and store counts. Shelf prices in stores were not read (A-48 to A-50).

Method · e-commerce record

The history on the E-commerce tab was read from PetWise operating plans, forecasts, results packs, board updates and e-commerce reviews of 2025 and 2026, and from the 2024 market assessment. Each figure was checked against the text of its document, events are dated to the nearest quarter, and the status of each failure is an advisor reading at 10 November 2026 (A-52, A-53).

Method · board presentations

The 2026 starting point, sales by channel, category and customer, the retailer asks and management’s 2027 plan come from the Q3 board meeting and the Product & Innovation presentation of 22 October 2026, with actuals to September and the last quarter at the 5+7 forecast. The starting point then sets the last quarter of e-commerce to its pace of shipments and its margin to 14 November (A-01, A-51, A-55, A-66).

Method · data gaps

October results, sales and margin targets for the 2027 launches, item contribution after ads and freight, item-level Amazon and Chewy sell-through after August, stock by item, incremental ad returns and store shelf shares after August 2024 were not available and should be closed first. The paid media dashboard fills part of the gap with retailer totals, brand fill rates and item breakevens to late October. Item-level marketplace data run to late August 2026 (Exhibit 4.86, A-57).

Method · run-rate convention

Values are annualised quarterly run-rates. A year’s EBITDA is the mean of its four quarters (A-02).

Sources

PetWise FY25–26 margin analysis, FY25 item actuals, 2026 AOP and 5+7, 13-week cash flow (30 Oct 2026), board decks 2025–26 including the Q3 and Product & Innovation presentations of 22 Oct 2026, the PetWise marketplace database (Amazon, Chewy, Walmart.com and Target.com, queried 9 and 13 Nov 2026), Chewy and Amazon analyses, the agency’s branded search review (17 Sep 2026), the PetWise paid media dashboard (data to 26 Oct 2026), Stackline dog-bed scorecards, Nielsen store scan data to 10 Aug 2024, retailer results and store counts, retailer and brand pages read 10 Nov 2026, ASINsight keyword reports, independent commercial and L.E.K. market studies, Outward Hound materials, public filings and benchmarks.

The packet answers each operating line of the assessment template.

The template asks the same questions of every company, in twelve functions, with six more for consumer products. Each line below shows the claim or reading the plan relies on, the result and the exhibits that answer it. Where the evidence is thin the line stays in the table with what is missing.

What holds. Every exhibit in the packet answers one line, so nothing is shown that the template does not ask for.

What to watch. The lines without enough evidence are mostly about people, suppliers and repeat purchase. The template’s function 10 and its ownership line deal with how a company is funded and owned, and they sit outside the scope of this packet.

Part 12 · Frequently asked questions

Questions a board asks about a plan like this.

Each answer opens with the short version, then the detail. Nothing here introduces a number that is not already in the packet.

Scope

What the packet covers and the period it uses.

Scope

It is an operating plan to take PetWise toward $10M of EBITDA, built from PetWise’s own data.

It covers commercial, operations, technology and AI levers, with their size, timing, owners and measures. The plan contains no acquisitions or disposals (the note below Exhibit 6.03). Figures are advisor estimates built on PetWise’s FY25 and 2026 data, its marketplace database and published benchmarks, and each one rests on an assumption in the register.

History runs to FY25 and 2026 actuals to September; the plan runs from Q4 2026 to Q4 2028.

FY25 item, brand and customer figures come from the FY25–26 gross margin analysis. The 2026 figures are actuals to September from the board presentations of 22 October 2026, with October to December at the 5+7 forecast; store-account detail is the 5+7 forecast. Marketplace figures run to 27 August 2026 for Amazon, to the week of 31 August for Chewy and to 8 November for the Walmart.com and Target.com seller accounts (Exhibit 4.82). Paid media figures and retailer sales totals run to 26 October 2026 (A-45). Plan values are annualised quarterly run-rates (A-02), shown by quarter in Exhibit 6.04.

Because 2026 includes one-time tariff refunds.

With actuals to September and the last quarter at forecast, 2026 shows about $0.3M of adjusted EBITDA, including $7.4M of tariff refunds booked in May, June and July. Net of the $1.0M of customer concessions the 5+7 set aside, the refunds add $6.4M, and removing them gives −$6.1M on the forecast. The forecast sets the last quarter of e-commerce 38% above the same quarter of 2025, and shipments since 1 October are running below that and at a lower product margin, so the packet takes $0.3M off for the sales pace and $0.3M for the margin rate. That gives the underlying −$6.7M that every bridge in the packet starts from (Exhibits 2.03, 2.30 and 2.09, A-01, A-55, A-66). The 5+7 alone gave −$4.4M; the difference is a weaker September, higher marketing and other costs, and a larger refund. The refunds do not repeat, so 2027 builds from the underlying figure.

A list of 49 operating questions, each with a result and the exhibits that answer it.

The same questions are asked of every company assessed this way. Exhibit 11.03 lists each one with the claim or reading the plan relies on and one of four results: supported, partly supported, contradicted or not enough evidence yet. A line without enough evidence says what is missing, and those requests sit beside the data gaps in Exhibit 11.02. The packet covers the operating business, so the lines on how a company is funded and owned are left out.

Reading the numbers

How to read the cases, run-rates and charts.

Interpretation

The plan case counts every lever at its planned value; the risk-adjusted case weights each one by confidence.

High, medium and low-confidence levers count at 90%, 70% and 50% of plan (A-03). The plan case reaches about $13M in 2028 and the risk-adjusted case about $6.2M, before any launch reserve (Exhibits 6.03 and 6.04). Management should run the business to the plan case, while the board judges progress against the risk-adjusted path at the gates in Exhibit 10.24.

The yearly EBITDA a lever adds once it is fully in place.

Each quarter’s run-rate is annualised. A year’s EBITDA is the mean of its four quarterly run-rates (A-02), which is why 2028 risk-adjusted EBITDA sits close to, but not exactly at, the Q4 2028 run-rate. Exhibit 6.15 shows how each initiative ramps quarter by quarter.

Because the plan exits loss-making lines and accounts before the growth levers ramp.

Exited lines and accounts, the item-tail cut, the one-off 2026 club volume and category erosion reduce 2027 gross sales. Cat, Chewy, Amazon, the FurHaven recovery and key-account programs add more than that back by 2028 (Exhibit 10.17, A-23).

They measure what shoppers bought at shelf prices, while PetWise reports what it invoiced.

Amazon shelf sales were $31.6M over the year to 27 August 2026 (Exhibit 4.76). PetWise invoiced less than that for the same units, because the retailer’s margin sits in between, and PetWise then pays allowances on top (A-27). Shoppers’ purchases also lead or lag PetWise’s shipments by a few weeks. The E-commerce part uses shelf sales for trends, and Exhibit 4.82 sets out what each source measures.

Inside the initiatives it supports, never on top.

Ten AI use cases enable about $10M of the $26M gross plan: demand forecasting inside AI planning and the Chewy plan, the content factory inside the digital shelf and the content-cost savings, pricing analytics inside revenue management, and so on (Exhibits 9.02 and 9.11, A-20). Removing a use case lowers the confidence of its initiative rather than subtracting a separate AI line.

Each opens on today’s case, and each slider stays inside a range the evidence supports.

There are seven. The plan simulator (Exhibit 10.08) moves delivery, timing and erosion on the plan model. The others each test one question: the 2026 starting point (Exhibit 2.13), sales per store (Exhibit 5.12), retail media (Exhibit 7.11), the FurHaven price reset (Exhibit 7.15), the item ceiling (Exhibit 8.02) and fill rates (Exhibit 8.09). In each, the buttons load named cases, the track under a result shows the full range the sliders can reach, and the tick marks the target, breakeven or lever the result is read against. Printing shows the cases as a table (A-36, A-47, A-63).

Because it is the whole packet in summary, and each of its charts is a copy of one proven later on.

The packet tells its story at three depths. The Overview gives each part’s main finding and one or two charts. Each part then opens with its own story, a headline and a storyboard of small pictures that link to the detail below. The detail sections carry the full evidence. Each chart re-draws an exhibit from that tab with the same values, sometimes at a smaller size, and its basis line names and links the exhibit it copies (Exhibit 1.05 re-draws Exhibit 5.01, for example).

The motion shows order and magnitude; the final frame is the exhibit.

Charts load as they come into view and animate once: lines draw in time order, bars grow from zero and table rows reveal in order. Hover any mark for the exact figure. If your device is set to reduce motion, the packet shows final values immediately, and printing shows every chart in its final state.

A range and a probability, where the risk-adjusted case gives one number.

The risk-adjusted case weights each lever once and assumes every date holds. The simulation draws lever size, capture, timing, erosion, retailer give-backs and the starting point 10,000 times (A-32 to A-35). Its middle outcome for 2028 is about $5.5M against about $6.2M for the risk-adjusted case, because slips and erosion lean to the downside, and it puts the chance of $10M or more at about 3% (Exhibits 10.03 and 10.34).

It is an estimate built on judgement, and it stayed between about 0% and 6% across the settings tested.

The capture spreads, the share of execution that is common to the levers and the chances of a late start are advisor judgements, not values fitted to PetWise history (A-33, A-34). Exhibit 10.35 re-runs the simulation with each one changed in turn. The reading that holds across them is that $10M in 2028 is unlikely on the plan as built, with or without a launch reserve, and that about 42% of runs reach $6M or more.

A sized launch reserve and more capture together bring it close to even, and neither does alone.

A launch reserve of about $5M of plan value, sized by gate one and delivered like a low-confidence lever, lifts the chance to about 22%. Ten more points of capture on each lever alone lifts it to about 16%, and both together to about 48% (Exhibit 10.04, A-37). The reserve counts at low confidence because recent launches have added little online: items first sold since July 2025 made about 5% of this year’s Amazon and Chewy shelf sales (Exhibit 4.84, A-56). The reserve is a what-if size. Its candidates are management’s 2027 launches and the options in Exhibit 3.57, none of which is yet sized in EBITDA. The simulator in Exhibit 10.08 shows the effect of other combinations of delivery, timing and erosion.

Data and assumptions

Where the data came from and what happens if it is wrong.

Provenance

The newest figures run to 14 November 2026.

Invoiced e-commerce sales, fill rates and stock run to 14 November (Exhibits 2.07 and 4.25, A-61). Shoppers’ purchases run to the week of 7 to 9 November on Amazon, Chewy and Walmart, and item by item to October (Exhibits 4.24 and 4.26, A-62). Walmart’s retail sales of PetWise brands run to 9 November (Exhibit 5.05, A-64). Item-level history in the marketplace database runs to late August 2026, company results to September 2026 and store shelf shares to August 2024.

From PetWise’s own systems and board materials, with outside sources for market context.

Internal figures come from the FY25–26 gross margin analysis, FY25 item-level actuals, the 2026 AOP and 5+7 plan, the 13-week cash flow, board decks and the marketplace database, which holds Amazon, Chewy, Walmart.com and Target.com sales by item. Market and peer figures come from NIQ, SmartScout, Stackline, ASINSIGHT, APPA, PLMA and Circana, and company filings. Brand-level competitor prices and ratings come from public retailer pages read on 10 November 2026 (A-38). Each exhibit names its source in its basis line.

Amazon and Chewy run to late August 2026, and the seller marketplaces to 12 November.

Item-level Amazon and Chewy data run to 27 and 31 August 2026 (Exhibit 4.86, A-57). The database holds no advertising, stock or fill-rate data, so it cannot show the October advertising changes or tell an out-of-stock item from a suppressed listing (Exhibit 4.82). The paid media dashboard fills part of that gap to 26 October, with ad returns, retailer sales totals and Amazon fill rates by brand (Exhibits 4.78 to 4.81). Two Chewy fields, returns and repeat units, changed meaning in December 2025 and are not used. Item-level September and October sell-through for Amazon and Chewy heads the data request list (Exhibit 11.02, A-28).

The capture rate matters most: each ten points moves 2028 EBITDA by about $2.6M.

Exhibit 10.30 shows 2028 EBITDA by capture and erosion. At 60% capture EBITDA is about $2M, still well above the 2026 underlying loss. Below about 90% capture, the $10M target needs the launch reserve, which is why gate one in June 2027 tests capture and the reserve early (A-03, A-04, A-37).

To check that each lever sits in a credible range, not to set its size.

Every lever is sized from PetWise’s own data first. Benchmarks such as McKinsey’s 10–20% gain in trade-spend effectiveness, BCG and Inverto’s up to 5% saving on direct spend, and McKinsey’s 20–50% cut in forecast error sit beside them as a reasonableness check. Exhibit 9.19 shows where the plan sits in each range, mostly at the low end.

Because shipments since 1 October are running below it.

The 5+7 sets October to December e-commerce at $14.8M of gross sales, 38% above the same quarter of 2025, while the year to September ran 24% below. In 2025 the last quarter was about 29% of the first nine months on PetWise’s shipments and about 35% on Amazon and Chewy sell-through; the forecast needs 52% (Exhibit 2.29). On last year’s pattern the quarter would land $4.1M to $6.6M below the forecast. Shipments have done better than that: $6.6M was invoiced from 1 October to 14 November against $7.3M in the forecast, as retailers restocked after this year’s stock-outs. On that pace the quarter lands $1.4M to $2.3M short, which takes $0.2M to $0.5M from EBITDA, and the packet uses $0.3M (Exhibit 2.30, A-55). Product margin on those shipments is also 2.5 to 3.0 points below the forecast rate, which takes a further $0.3M (Exhibit 2.09, A-66). Sales figures for 2026 stay on the forecast view. Shoppers’ purchases are still below last year, so the restocking should not be carried into 2027.

It runs from 2022 to 10 August 2024, and it is the oldest evidence in the packet.

Brand shares in stores come from store scan data cut for a market assessment PetWise commissioned in 2024 (A-49). Target, Petco and Walmart have changed their pet shelves since. PetWise’s own account sales run to FY25 and the 2026 forecast, and the retailers’ statements to autumn 2026 (A-48). Exhibit 5.28 lists what current scan data would replace.

They use different prices: about 5x on list prices and 4.6x on the prices shoppers paid.

The PetWise workbook gives 4.95x on Amazon and 5.22x on Chewy on list prices (A-12). The paid media dashboard uses realized prices and the item margin file of 13 July 2026, which gives 4.6x on Amazon, 5.6x on Chewy and 12.2x at Walmart (A-43). Walmart’s figure is high because its July ad mix sat on low-margin items, and the margin file’s own figure for advertisable Walmart items is 7.5x (Exhibit 7.38).

Public retailer pages, most read on 10 November 2026, with third-party estimates for Amazon.

Chewy, Walmart.com, PetSmart and brand pages were read on one day, so some prices were promotional (A-38). Two reads are older: Hot Pursuit at Walmart, from a page dated about September 2026, and Litter-Robot, from April 2026. Amazon pages could not be read, so Amazon prices, ratings and unit sales are ASINsight estimates for March to August 2026. Dog-bed shares come from Stackline scorecards for early 2025 (A-39). Exhibit 3.59 lists each source and the gap to close.

Most follow stated cut-offs on the hero item, and the claim score is a judgement.

Price, rating, review depth and price consistency are scored against the cut-offs in Exhibit 3.41. Amazon category search follows a stated scale from the top-ten lists read, and the claim score is advisor judgement from listing text (A-40). The choice of hero item matters: SmartyKat scores 22 on its catnip mice and 19 on Hot Pursuit. The order of the strongest and weakest brands is therefore more reliable than the size of the gaps between them.

From PetWise’s own board documents of 2025 and 2026 and the 2024 market assessment.

Exhibit 4.49 lists each document, what it gave and how it was checked. Yearly sales, plans, contribution, orders cut and advertising were read from the text of the operating plans, forecasts, results packs and board updates (A-52). Events are dated to the nearest quarter and the status of each failure is an advisor reading at 10 November 2026 (A-53). Current-year figures come from the marketplace database and the paid media dashboard, as on the Marketplace evidence and Commercial tabs. Figures that appear only inside chart images in those documents were not re-read for this tab.

Findings

The questions the findings raise.

Findings

FurHaven is most of the online decline, and cat earns the best margins.

FurHaven lost $9.5M of the $12.9M fall in online shelf sales (Exhibit 4.90), and its decline tracks shelf-price rises that a terms reset can reverse (Exhibits 4.17 and 7.13). Cat brands earn 23% to 32% gross margin against 20% for FurHaven (Exhibit 7.03), and Amazon cat sales grew about three times as fast as dog (Exhibit 3.09). So the FurHaven reset runs through 2027 to stop the loss, while new investment goes to cat.

On the same items, shelf prices rose far more than PetWise’s prices to the retailers.

FurHaven shelf prices rose about 7% on Chewy and 5% on Amazon, while what the retailers paid PetWise moved about 1% (Exhibit 4.74). The data cannot say why. A higher suggested price, fewer funded promotions and a retailer seeking margin would each look the same, and Chewy earned about 4% on FurHaven before allowances (Exhibit 4.18). Management should confirm the cause before the terms reset is negotiated (A-30).

Because store brands and China-direct sellers set the price floor there.

Retailer brands hold 85% to 92% of mass-channel dog furniture, crates and litter boxes, and China-based sellers hold 61% to 67% of key Amazon categories (Exhibit 3.12). Matching them would mean selling at their cost base without their scale. The plan leaves those items and puts the effort into differentiated, review-rich products.

No: fewer than 600 items make most of the sales, and the tail loses money.

In FY25, 549 items made 80% of gross sales and 837 items lost $5.3M of gross margin (Exhibits 2.05 and 2.21). Online, 1,367 Amazon items made 5% of sales over the last year (Exhibit 4.76). Cuts follow the five tests in Exhibit 8.13, starting with contribution after allowances and freight, so small but profitable items stay (A-13, A-14).

Chewy has stabilised and is growing outside FurHaven, while FurHaven on Amazon is still falling.

Chewy’s gap to last year narrowed from 31% to 11% during 2026, and sales outside FurHaven are 12% above last year (Exhibit 4.32). Chewy hardgoods grew 14.4% in its latest quarter (Exhibit 3.28). Amazon stays important, but is run for profit: about 300 hero listings, ads above breakeven and reset terms (Exhibit 7.21).

Because PetWise’s seller account there sells about $0.3M a year and is shrinking.

Walmart.com and Target.com seller sales total under $1M a year, Walmart.com fell 22% from April to October, and Walmart Fulfillment Services has delivered $12K since March 2025 (Exhibits 4.64 and 4.77). The plan treats both as a capped test with a 2028 target of about $1.8M (Exhibit 7.21, A-10). The larger opportunity on Walmart.com runs through the Walmart buying team, and management is moving the seller items to Walmart’s own buying, with more than 350 items planned.

Chew manufacturing moves to contract makers, with a written Topco contract agreed first.

Management’s scenarios range from a small transfer to a full shutdown (Exhibit 8.15). The plan favours exiting manufacturing with two contract makers, because the sole rawhide partner is in distress. Management is bringing that partner, Santa Fe, on as a finished-goods supplier by March 2027 and plans one manufacturing hub by June 2027, so a second maker matters more. Topco is the largest customer of the plant, so supply continuity is a condition of the exit, and the risk trigger in Exhibit 10.22 watches its fill rate (A-16). Pet Factory chews also held their Amazon sales and grew on Chewy (Exhibit 4.68), and the new Chip Dips carry a US-made flag, so online supply and the origin claim are part of the same condition.

They can, which is why the plan trades cuts for commitments rather than asking for them outright.

PetWise offers in-stock, forecast-accuracy and content commitments in return for lower allowances on hero items (Exhibits 7.23 and 7.27). If no agreement is reached by the end of the first quarter of 2027, the plan shifts to item-level exits on the accounts concerned (Exhibit 10.22, A-07). Retailers are also asking for part of the tariff refund back. The plan carries about $1M a year of recurring give-backs and answers each ask with a trade for placement or terms (Exhibit 7.02, A-51).

It supports most levers and pulls against three.

The first-year strategy and 2027 product slate shown to the board on 22 October 2026 build several of the plan’s positions: the FurHaven ladder, rechargeable cat toys, a collagen chew, cat-first carriers, price enforcement, ocean consolidation and better forecasts. Three moves pull the other way: a target of doubling sales to $300M or more by 2030, a range that adds several hundred items without exits, and advertising that grows ahead of tested returns (Exhibits 6.23 and 6.18). The launches carry no sales, margin or price target yet, so the plan counts them only as candidates for the launch reserve (A-37).

Price, fulfilment, advertising, listings and the team failed one after another, and each plan assumed a rebound.

E-commerce gross sales fell from $91.9M in 2023 to about $43.3M on the latest view of 2026 (Exhibit 4.01). Lower-priced rivals took FurHaven’s share of Amazon bedding first (Exhibit 4.15). Orders were then cancelled and cut for lack of stock (Exhibit 4.19), advertising was cut by about half in 2025 and restored at returns below breakeven (Exhibits 4.20 and 4.31), best-selling items were delisted, and the channel changed leader and agency (Exhibit 4.38). Five of the eight strands on the timeline are still open (Exhibit 4.05), and Exhibit 4.39 pairs each failure with the lever that addresses it.

Profit first on the few hundred items that carry the sales, then growth, with weekly measures.

257 Amazon items and 203 Chewy items make most of each channel’s shelf sales. Five levers act mainly online and carry $4.8M at plan, about $3.6M weighted for risk (Exhibit 4.34, A-54). The first actions are dated in Exhibits 4.35 and 4.46, each failure has a measure that shows when it is closed (Exhibit 4.47), and the plan leads with Chewy while Amazon is run for profit (Exhibit 7.21).

Yes. Store accounts are about 70% of sales, and the Stores tab reads them from account, shelf and retailer evidence.

Account sales and margins come from PetWise’s plans and margin files (Exhibits 5.04 and 5.21). Brand shares on the store shelf come from store scan data to August 2024, where retailer own brands held 61% of bedding (Exhibit 5.07). Retailer positions come from their published results (Exhibit 5.26). Prices and ratings were read on retailer websites, so the price of each brand on the physical shelf is not assessed (A-38).

It widens the retail media lever from Amazon to three retailers and names the first cuts.

Ads returned 4.31x at Walmart, 3.30x at Amazon and 3.26x at Chewy in October to date, against breakevens of about 12.2x, 4.6x and 5.6x (Exhibit 7.10). 73 items under 60% of breakeven lose about $0.9M a year after ads, close to the lever’s $1.0M plan value (Exhibit 7.32, A-44). The plan value and the odds are unchanged. September’s shortfall of about $284K before halo suggests room above the plan value, which hold-out tests would confirm.

No. It should stop the named items first and test the rest.

Breakeven counts ad-attributed sales and leaves out the lift ads give to search rank and other sales (A-43). 89 items clear breakeven and can take more budget, and FurHaven items that pay back on Chewy had their ads cut (Exhibit 7.39). The rule works item by item: cut under 60% of breakeven, fix between 60% and 100%, hold or scale above it, and use hold-out tests to measure what attributed returns miss.

It sharpens levers already in the plan and supplies candidates for a reserve.

Most moves in Exhibit 3.26 are the practical content of existing levers: the FurHaven price reset, cat growth, the digital shelf and retail media. Six further options in Exhibit 3.57 are not counted in plan value. Two overlap existing levers and would count only above those levers’ plan values. The six are candidates for the reserve tested in Exhibit 10.04 (A-37, A-42).

Branded search spend was cut by about two-thirds in July 2026.

Branded spend fell about 64% while total spend rose about 29%, and FurHaven’s share of the shelf on its own brand searches fell from about 67% in June to about 30% in August (Exhibit 3.21). Brand terms had returned 5.2x before the change, against 1.2x in August on the category terms that replaced them (Exhibit 3.47, A-41). Restoring brand defence belongs inside the retail media lever. The review measures shelf, and the effect on sales is not measured.

Next steps

What happens next and how progress is tracked.

Process

Seven decisions, a working value office and the wave-one actions.

The decisions are an item ceiling that nets the 2027 launches against exits, the sizing of each launch and of the product-transition cash, the e-commerce profit rules with hold-out tests and relisting of the dark cat items, the answer to each retailer give-back ask, the Mundelein exit with the McAllen and Quarry renewals, the revenue management launch with FurHaven tier prices, and the value office with the first senior hire (Exhibit 10.13). The hundred-day plan in Exhibit 10.19 sets the actions by workstream.

Through ten monthly measures, weekly online measures and dated stage gates.

The scorecard in Exhibit 10.11 pairs outcomes, EBITDA and gross margin, with the drivers that lead them, and Exhibit 10.27 adds online measures read weekly from the marketplace database. Gate one in June 2027 tests monthly breakeven, item count, allowances and whether the launch reserve has been sized; gate two in December 2027 tests a run-rate of about $8M; gate three in June 2028 tests about $10M (Exhibit 10.24).

A named executive owns each initiative, and a value office tracks progress weekly.

Exhibit 10.18 lists the owner, first milestone and KPI for each initiative. The governance rhythm in Exhibit 10.20 runs from weekly stand-ups to the monthly board scorecard. Incentives in Exhibit 10.26 tie pay to EBITDA, cash and each owner’s own driver.

It kept McAllen as it is and flagged a large cash need for product transitions.

Management ruled out combining the McAllen buildings and will renew on a 3-year term, so the footprint lever rests on Mundelein and El Paso (A-16). It estimates about $15M of cash for product transitions by the end of the first quarter of 2027, which turns 2027 program cash negative until it is sized (Exhibit 6.09, A-26). Excess stock has fallen to about $5.5–6.0M, but liquidation recovers about 20% of cost (Exhibit 8.10, A-19).

Missing a gate triggers a defined response rather than a new plan.

If gate one is missed, the next wave of cost actions is pulled forward, and if the launch reserve has not been sized by then, the 2028 target is reset. If gate two is missed, the board adds levers, starting with deeper item and account exits. A further duty increase, a lost line review or a large retailer give-back each has its own trigger and response in Exhibit 10.22.
